en: Preface to the Divine Jewel of the Pure Land Dharma Gate The reason the Pure Land Dharma Gate is called the "Divine Jewel" (shenzhu) is that the Buddha’s virtues are perfectly integrated and manifest according to the mind, just like a *maṇi* gem;
whatever one vows for will surely be fulfilled. As the *Amitābha Sūtra* states: "The ocean of the Tathāgatas' right and universal knowledge arises from the thoughts and mind."
Therefore, when one contemplates the Buddha with the mind, this very mind is the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics;

this mind creates the Buddha, and this mind is the Buddha. Since it is said that "this mind creates the Buddha" and "this mind is the Buddha," one knows that this mind creates the nine realms and this mind is the nine realms.
Among all worldly and world-transcending phenomena, there are none that are not produced by the mind. None.
It is not identical to the mind, yet it is not other than it. Thus, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "Know that its fundamental cause arises according to its conditions.
All phenomena that arise are manifested solely by the mind. In this way, the empty space of the ten directions and the lands as numerous as motes of dust are all things within the mind;
apart from the mind, not a single dharma can be found. Therefore, one knows that throughout the ten periods of time, from the beginning to the end...
Without departing from the present thought, the boundless oceans of lands are not separated from oneself by so much as a hair’s breadth.
The distant reaches of ten trillion lands are precisely the Pure Land of the Mind-only; the eighty-four thousand wondrous marks are none other than Amitābha of one's own fundamental nature.
Previously, I set aside the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss to speak separately of the Pure Land of the Mind-only, setting aside the [external] myriad...

O Venerable One of Compassionate Virtue! To speak specifically of the Amitābha of intrinsic nature: to turn one's back on the Compassionate Father of the Land of Bliss and fall into the deep pit of the waters of death—how truly lamentable this is!
Out of longing for the Great Master [Huiyuan], he completely abandoned his former habits and exerted himself to investigate this school.
Seeing the erroneous interpretations of his contemporaries and taking pity on his own past errors, he compiled the sincere words of various sages to elucidate the wondrousness of the One Vehicle.

This is its essential meaning. It is titled *The Divine Pearl of the Pure Land*. It is intended for those who practice the path of the Pure Land so that they may realize that the single thought-moment of the present moment possesses immeasurable significance.
They should have faith that the Buddha Amitābha and his environment exist within the Western Land, yet that this Western Land and its environment do not depart from one's own fundamental nature.
To direct the spirit toward billions of lands is, in truth, to be born within one’s own mind; to conceive form within the nine lotuses—how could this escape the span of a single kṣaṇa?
The profound meaning of the "Divine Jewel" (Shenzhu) truly lies herein. I, deeply ashamed of my own ignorance, have no words worthy of praise;
I merely record what I heard directly from him to manifest the Master’s intent. Written by the student of Pure Land practice, Fanghui, in the summer of the Ren-shen year.

What is the "Divine Pearl of the Pure Land"? It refers to the nature of the mind in this very moment, which is wondrous and unfathomable.
This is why the *Amitābha Sūtra* speaks of "inconceivable merit" and how it is "protected and remembered by all Buddhas.
This is also why the sages and worthies of past and present have exerted their utmost strength to propagate the Treasure-King Samādhi. This mind—
As for "nature" (*dharmatā*): it is fundamentally vertical in its depth and horizontal in its pervasiveness; it is neither born nor extinguished.
It primordially possesses the pure and wondrous lands of the Buddhas of the ten directions. Therefore, the Western Pure Land of Amitābha truly exists, perfectly present within this very realm.

Alas, sentient beings have heavy obstructions and are unable to perceive it; thus, the Teacher of the Sahā world has toiled to open the gate of expedient means, as have the World-Honored Ones of the ten directions.

He extends his broad and long tongue. Thus, the *Miaozong* states: "The mind-treasury contains all phenomena; how could it have any boundaries? Yet, lacking the conditions for wondrous contemplation, they remain hidden and do not manifest.
Now, relying on the Buddha’s words, one should contemplate them in accordance with their nature: the radiance of the jewel-ground and its various extraordinary marks."
It manifests in accordance with the mind. The *Zonglun* states: "The single thought-moment of the present extends through all antiquity and reaches unto the present;
therefore, it is named 'Immeasurable Life' (*Amitāyus*). It is spiritually luminous and penetratingly clear; therefore, it is named 'Immeasurable Light' (*Amitābha*).

If one can indeed maintain the name of Amitābha Buddha in every thought-moment, this is precisely to realize Immeasurable Life and radiate Immeasurable Light in every thought-moment. Thus, the fruit and the cause interpenetrate, subtle and wondrous beyond measure."

I reflect: the protection and mindfulness of all Buddhas reside herein. Thus, one should know that the Pure Land is the supreme essential of the mind, like a wish-fulfilling jewel that instantaneously contains all treasures;
how could there be any further doubt? I regret that although I have long admired the Pure Land, I did not understand its true nature.
Whenever I questioned my fellow Chan practitioners, they would all say, "The Pure Land is but the pure mind; Amitābha is one's own nature. One must not cling to appearances."
Therefore, although I delighted in the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha, I was merely attached to emptiness.

Later, upon reading the teachings of the Tiantai and Pure Land schools as well as the *Wusheng lun* (Treatise on Non-arising), I finally realized that the manifest reality of the Pure Land is precisely the manifestation of one's own mind, and that the true body of Amitābha appears therein.

This is precisely the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). There truly exists a Pure Land where one may be born; there truly exists Amitābha who may be seen. Therefore, it is said: "Birth is fundamentally non-birth;

one gives birth to the four lands. Seeing is yet free from seeing; one sees the three bodies (*trikāya*). From this point forward, with a dead mind, one should recite the Buddha's name and seek rebirth.
I have respectfully compiled these essential words on the *Awakening of Faith* from my humble views into this brief collection. May I encourage myself with it and inform those of like mind.
My wish is that you may broaden the eyes of your understanding and enter deeply into the gates of practice. A single phrase of Amitābha encompasses the inexhaustible ocean of the Buddha’s merits;
one should contemplate its perfect realization. This is what Śākyamuni exhorted and praised, and what all Buddhas proclaim in unison. Any who possess faith [should not...]
It is not that one fails to exert the mind and practice with diligence.
In the *Wǎngshēng Jìngtǔ Juéyíwén* (Text for Resolving Doubts about Rebirth in the Pure Land), the Great Master Cíyún [states]:
"The ten directions of the pure and the defiled are all gathered together within a single kṣaṇa; in a single thought-moment, form and mind are arrayed and fully encompassed."
The Dharma-realm is, in its entirety, inherently and spontaneously possessed; it is not newly formed through dependent origination.
As it is so within a single thought-moment, so it is within a single atom. Thus, within each and every atom are all lands; within each and every mind are all minds.

Each mind and each atom further interpenetrate one another, layer upon layer, infinitely and without obstruction, manifesting instantaneously and all at once, neither hidden nor revealed—everything is perfectly complete.
Thus, there is neither superiority nor inferiority. If a divine pearl suddenly contains all manner of jewels, it is like the Indra’s net where a thousand lights reflect one another;

since my own mind is thus, the bodies of sentient beings and Buddhas are equal. Only when one realizes this can the spirit be turned toward billions of lands, for they truly arise within one's own heart.

How could the nine lotuses of the womb-essence escape the limit of a single *kṣaṇa*? If phenomena and principle were separated and purity and defilement obstructed one another, how could ordinary beings who have committed the five heinous crimes ascend to the Treasure Land through ten recitations, and how could the worthy ones of the Two Vehicles reach the Golden Pond upon turning their minds?
To believe in this perfect teaching, there is nothing that cannot be attained; to be ignorant of this ultimate principle, everything encountered leads to delusion. [The Lotus Sutra...]
Yan said: "The mind is like a skilled painter, creating the various five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). Within all worlds, there is nothing that is not created by the mind.
As it is with the mind, so it is with the Buddha; as it is with the Buddha, so it is with sentient beings. Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction.
The *Treatise on the Awakening of Faith* states: "That which is called 'Dharma' refers to the mind of sentient beings. This mind encompasses all worlds."

It encompasses both mundane and supramundane dharmas; based upon this, the meaning of Mahāyāna (Mahāyāna is the Great Vehicle; if it were not for this mind, how could one possibly be conveyed by it) is revealed through the sixteen contemplations.
All Buddhas are the body of the Dharma-realm, entering into the thoughts and minds of all sentient beings, even to the point that "this mind creates the Buddha" and "this mind is the Buddha.
This is the Pratyutpanna Samādhi: "The Buddha is my own mind; it is by means of my own mind that I see the Buddha."
Regarding such statements as "My mind shall become a Buddha," those who discuss this principle find it brilliantly elucidated throughout the Mahāyāna sūtras.

As for the wondrous *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the Tathāgata personally records rebirth therein; and in the sudden teaching of the *Avataṃsaka*, Samantabhadra personally sets forth the dedication of merit.

Thus we know that while Amitābha was on the stage of a bodhisattva, he contemplated this principle and made great vows to universally embrace all beings; and now that Śākyamuni has attained fruition, he extols this very principle.
With his broad tongue, he praised this profoundly; throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time, there was no one who did not agree. He asked:
"Regarding the wondrous principle of perfect consummation, must all people of the world first undergo contemplative practice before [the Pure Land] arises? He replied: "Not so.

Now, I shall simply resolve your doubts directly, so that you may know that the adornments of the hundred jewels of the Pure Land and the causes and effects of the nine grades are both present within the infinitesimal thought of sentient beings, fully endowed within their fundamental nature."

Only then does one attain the practical application for rebirth; it occurs spontaneously according to one's vows. This is to pervade the ten directions without departing from the present thought-moment, traversing the dharma-realm in perfect accord with the mind-only principle.
To avoid falling into the common stream of belief that clings to "this" while rejecting "that," one must understand that the nine grades of rebirth each have their own distinct types of practice.
Regarding the three grades of the superior class, both understanding and practice are required; thus it is said: "You must practice the Mahāyāna and understand..."
Regarding the primary meaning: when scholars see the worthy, they think of emulating them; aspiring to ascend the golden throne, one should take refuge in wondrous contemplation.
As for the six grades of intermediate and lower birth through causes, it merely requires the diligent observance of prohibitive precepts and the practice of worldly benevolence and compassion.

Even for those of the very lowest grade, who are originally wicked and rebellious, if they maintain ten sincere recitations, they shall immediately be born in that land. One need only know that the Pure Land exists, and all may attain it.

This refers to the "turning of the mind" (huíxīn). Although worldly people may claim that the Pure Land school belongs to the Mahāyāna, they cannot distinguish it according to the teachings as described above; thus, they fail to escape confusion and cannot resolve their doubts.
Verses on Right Faith and Aspiration from the Amitābha Sūtra:
I prostrate to the Buddhas of the ten directions, To Amitābha, the most honored among the holy ones, And to the Vaipulya sūtras, The treasury of all the jewels of the Dharma.
To Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and the assembly of great Bodhisattvas, with a heart of sincere faith,

I have carved woodblocks and printed copies of the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* and the *Gāthā of Right Faith*, each totaling ten thousand copies, to bestow upon the fourfold assembly for their acceptance and recitation.
The verses are for inspiring faith; the sūtras are for supporting recitation and study.

If one recites at least three fascicles each day, one will complete one thousand and eighty fascicles in a year, and ten thousand and eight hundred in ten years—how much more so for those who recite even more, or over many more years?

Thus have I accumulated merit, and naturally I shall be born before the Buddha. Wherever these ten thousand scrolls of my scriptures are circulated, may at least one person recite and uphold them to be reborn in the Pure Land.
By the power of this merit, I vow that I shall certainly be born in that land.
How much more so for many people! Though a person may pass away, the scripture remains; as it is transmitted and passed down from one to another, this is called the "Inexhaustible Lamp.
Lamp after lamp illuminates one another, shattering the long night of birth and death, revealing the Bodhi of the Buddhas, until all beings ultimately attain birth therein together.
In the eternally quiescent and luminous Pure Land, I take this pure merit and dedicate it to my sovereign and my parents.
May our nation’s sage emperors and sage queens enjoy ten thousand years of benevolent longevity each, nurturing all classes of beings; may my own parents and kinsmen likewise do so.
Whether enemies or kin, those who are neither enemy nor kin—may they all rely upon these supreme roots of goodness and be reborn together in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (Sukhāvatī).

Although the words and phrases of this *Amitābha Sūtra* are concise, its intent is identical to that of the *Larger Sūtra*. The sublime sages respond to conditions; it is only the brevity or extensiveness that differs. Relying on...

The primary subject and its attendants are fully present herein. Regarding the methods of aspiration and practice, this work surpasses other expositions; its phrasing is concise yet its meaning is vast, and it is precisely because of this that chanting it yields great merit.

First, it extensively praises the environment and the beings therein to inspire sentient beings to seek them with joy. Second, it cites examples from the six directions to provide uniform instruction and encourage the development of faith.
Third, it presents the difficult by way of comparison with the easy, enabling those who hear it to know where to take refuge. This is the first [chapter].

Regarding the extensive praise of the primary and secondary environments (*āśraya* and *adhiṣṭhāna*): first there is the praise, followed by the exhortation to cultivate the vows and practices. From "The Buddha addressed the Elder... onwards, the subject of the praise is established.
From "Why is that land named Sukhāvatī? onwards, the praise of the resultant environment (*phala-adhiṣṭhāna*) begins:

(1) jeweled nets adorn the heavens and jade forests rise from the earth; (2) the ponds flow with the eight virtues of water and lotuses emit four kinds of light; (3) celestial music resonates throughout the six periods of the day, and [the robes] hang from the shoulders...
Flowers are scattered across billions of lands. (3) Transformed birds expound the categories of the Path, and wind-swept trees transmit the sounds of the Dharma.
(4) Within your mind, Śāriputra, you have extensively praised the primary retribution;

first, you praised the Transformation Lord, whose eighty thousand marks and signs encompass all radiance, and whose merit is likened to the sands of the Ganges, with his lifespan summarized as ten kalpas since attaining Buddhahood. (5) To exclude what is past...

"Furthermore, there is no need to resolve doubts" (the above concerns the spiritual leader). Next, from "Moreover, Śāriputra" onwards, the retinue is praised. Although the śrāvakas are numerous, they have all resolved upon the Great Mind;

although the bodhisattvas are many, they mostly occupy the stage of the "Successor. Those born [in this land] all return to the Determined Assembly, and those setting out on the path immediately join the stage of Non-retrogression (the above concerns the retinue).
Next, from "Furthermore, when sentient beings hear [this]" onwards, it exhorts the cultivation of vows and practices. First, the vow; next, the practice.

"Even with minor roots of goodness, one may practice through humble cultivation. Regarding the phrase "for even a single day," this refers precisely to the thickness or thinness of one's application of the mind, not to the length or brevity of the time.
One should follow the principle of "single-mindedness without distraction. The passage beginning with "When such a person approaches the end of life" clarifies the attainment of the fruit.

The section beginning with "I see this benefit" concludes with an exhortation. Next, the passage beginning with "As I am now" constitutes the second part, which cites the six directions as examples of commonality.

To instruct and inspire faith: first, he cites examples of those who attained [the goal] together with him; next, under the section "In your mind," he exhorts one to believe, which is also an exhortation to uphold [the teaching].

From "As I am now" onwards is the third section, which uses what is difficult to illustrate what is easy: attaining the Way amidst the five turbidities is difficult, whereas practicing in the Pure Land is easy—as stated in the text.
I request that you first carefully examine these structural divisions, and then recite the text; thus, the beginning and end will follow a logical order, and your merit will be realized.

It is not in vain. For instance, whether at the break of dawn or in the stillness of night, one may withdraw the senses to sit upright, reciting with the mouth and roaming with the mind, allowing the spirit to roam freely within the profound depths.
Thus, defilements are cleansed and the pure realm is no longer lost. How could it not be so, as the broad tongue encourages its upholding?
The Gate of Binding One’s Conditions for Rebirth in the Pure Land:
Regarding this gate, whether in public affairs or private life, and throughout the engagement with various worldly duties, one should never forget the Buddha even in moments of haste or distraction.
Furthermore, when recollecting the Pure Land, it is like being focused on a pressing matter; even while engaged in various activities, one does not fail to secretly keep that prior matter in mind.

Recollecting the Buddha is also like this: if mindfulness is lost, one repeatedly gathers it back. After a long time, this becomes one's nature, such that one constantly recollects it spontaneously and effortlessly.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "For example, suppose there is one person who is exclusively intent on remembering, and another person who is exclusively prone to forgetting.
These two people may not meet even when they encounter one another, or they may see one another yet it is as if they do not see.

Yet, because these two people remember each other and their mutual remembrance is deep, this continues from birth to birth until they are like a form and its shadow, never becoming separated or different. The Tathāgatas of the ten directions regard all sentient beings with compassion..."

A mother remembers her son; yet if the son has fled and gone away, what is the use of her remembering him? If the son remembers his mother as much as the mother remembers him, then throughout their successive lives, mother and son shall not be separated by great distance.
If the minds of sentient beings remember the Buddha and contemplate the Buddha, they will certainly see the Buddha in the present and in the future.

They will not be far from the Buddha, and without relying on expedient means, they will spontaneously attain the opening of the mind. It is like a person who is smeared with incense; their body [is perfumed].
It possesses a fragrance. By fixing the mind in this manner, one spontaneously and constantly wards off all evil thoughts.

Even if one intends to commit an evil act, because of the recollection of the Buddha, that evil cannot be accomplished. Even when following along with the commission of an evil deed, the mind remains constantly humble and soft;

just as a body with fragrance naturally becomes free from stench, so too, upon perceiving even a slight arising of an evil thought in the mind, one immediately recollects the Buddha. By means of the Buddha...
By the power [of this practice], evil thoughts will naturally subside. It is like a person encountering hardship who seeks a powerful ally and will certainly be delivered from it.

Furthermore, when seeing others suffer, one uses the mind of mindfulness of the Buddha to feel compassion for them, wishing that they be free from suffering. If one encounters the execution of criminal punishment, because of mindfulness of the Buddha, a heart of pity arises;
one vows to be reborn in the Pure Land and pledges to rescue one another. In passing through all circumstances, [one maintains this practice].

Whether they be wholesome or unwholesome, all realms [of karma] are transformed by recollecting the Buddha with the mind; because one forms vows through mental recollection, the *Samantabhadra-praṇidhāna-rāja* states:
"All evil deeds shall not be accomplished, while all wholesome karmas shall be fully harmonized. This is precisely that meaning.
In this manner, through continuous practice, mindfulness of the Buddha remains in the mind, capable of accomplishing all causes and merits of purity.
Fearing that it would weary the reader, I shall not elaborate further; truly, this gateway is of the greatest benefit.
Preface to the Ritual for Repentance and Vows for Rebirth in the Pure Land:
Tracing its origins, the Buddhas, out of compassion for sentient beings who are deluded and blind, established numerous skillful means to guide and lead them.

Yet, among all these, the practice of pure karma for the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang) alone is swift and direct to cultivate. All Mahāyāna sūtras proclaim this essential point; there are no Buddhas of the ten directions who do not [endorse it].

This is a method praised by all. Whether they be bhikṣus, the fourfold assembly, or virtuous men and women—whether their faculties are impaired or complete—if they wish to swiftly shatter the various darknesses of ignorance, and wish to eternally extinguish the grave offenses of the five heinous acts, the ten evil deeds, and violations of the prohibitions, as well as other minor transgressions, they should cultivate this dharma.
If they wish to restore the pure precepts of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, they shall attain mindfulness in the present.
Those who wish to master the Buddha-samādhis and all the gates of the pāramitās of the bodhisattvas should study this Dharma.
Those who desire to be free from all fears at the time of death, with body and mind peaceful and at ease, experiencing joy like returning home;

whose dwellings are illuminated by light and filled with extraordinary fragrances and music; and before whom Amitābha Buddha, Avalokiteśvara, and Mahāsthāmaprāpta appear in person to escort them with purple-golden [lotuses], should study this Dharma.
A platform where hands are extended to receive and guide; where the five paths are cut across and the nine grades are brought to rest. Shedding the heat of affliction, one finds peace in coolness.

Having first departed from worldly toil, one immediately reaches the stage of non-retrogression. Without passing through long kalpas, one attains the state of non-arising—this is the Dharma one should study.
If one wishes to cultivate even a small portion of this Dharma and thereby evoke a wondrous response, the Buddhas of the ten directions will all simultaneously offer praise, appearing before one.
He received a prophecy of his future enlightenment. In a single thought-moment, he made offerings to innumerable Buddhas and immediately returned to his own land.

There, he sat and ate together with Amitābha, engaged in discourse with Avalokiteśvara, and followed the footsteps of Mahāsthāmaprāpta. His eyes and ears saw and heard through all things; his physical stature was boundless, and he moved freely through the air.

He possessed perfect knowledge of his past lives and perceived the five realms of existence as clearly as images reflected in a mirror. In every moment of thought, he realized and entered the inexhaustible samādhis.
[This is] obscure. Such descriptions could not be fully exhausted. One should cultivate this supreme Dharma. As it has been taught, all is true and not false.
The Buddhas of the ten directions extend their broad and long tongues to praise this matter, demonstrating its non-deceptiveness.
How could we, then, dare not believe the Buddha? Now, taking the various sutras concerning the Pure Land, I establish this method of practice. If...
Preface to the Brief Tradition of Rebirth in the Western Land: Those who desire broad knowledge and seek the benefits found within the scriptures should look to the Western Pure Land.
There, amidst jade forests and jeweled nets, pearl pavilions and the Jasper Pond, it transcends billions of buddha-fields with its radiant white tuft.
Illuminating a thousand rays throughout the *sāhasra-lokadhātus*, he is praised by all Buddhas and revered by the multitude of sages. Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī both vow to be born in his land;
Vasubandhu and Maitreya both pledge to travel to that direction. If even the Great Sages act thus, how much more so should ordinary beings?

As for the scattering of causes and the fixing of karma, where even a small good deed yields great merit—one cuts off the five paths and gallops toward eternal liberation, casting a longing gaze back [upon this world].
Those of the nine grades ascend ever higher until they reach the stage of *sāmayika-samyaktva*, from which there is no further regression. Thus, the original vow of that Buddha states:

"If, when I attain Buddhahood, sentient beings of the ten directions who with sincere heart believe and rejoice, desiring to be born in my land, should not be reborn there even after ten recitations, may I not attain perfect enlightenment—except for those who commit the five heinous crimes or slander the true Dharma. Now, as it is fortunate that we have committed none of these heinous crimes...
As for the sin of not slandering the Mahāyāna: how could there be a wish that is not fulfilled? Furthermore, the *Sixteen Contemplations* states:

"Those of the lowest grade of rebirth are possessed of all manner of sins, including the four grave offenses and the five heinous crimes, and they slander the Vaipulya teachings; yet when the fires of hell appear before them..."
If one recites the Buddha’s name ten times, the fierce fires of hell will transform into a cool breeze, and one will be reborn in that land.

This thus permits even those who have committed grave offenses to attain rebirth through ten recitations; how much more so for those without such sins? Inferring from this, each person should have confidence:
all who aspire to be born there shall have their wishes fulfilled. Therefore, the Great Master Tiantai Zhiyi praised at the time of his death: [The fourth...]

The Eighteenth Vow adorns the Pure Land with lotus ponds and jeweled trees; yet, though it is easy to go there, no one does so. Even when the signs of the fiery chariot appear, if one repents for a single thought-moment, one may still attain rebirth.
How much more so for those who cultivate through precepts and meditative concentration, and whose power from practicing the pure path is truly not in vain.

Furthermore, his original vow states: "If sentient beings of the ten directions, upon hearing my name, fix their mindfulness upon my land and dedicate their merit with the desire to be born there, yet do not succeed in doing so, I vow not to attain Buddhahood.
Moreover, one should compare the duration and proximity of karmic practices:
if even ten moments of mindful recollection and joyful faith lead to birth in that land, how much more so for those who possess such faith for a single day, or for a month, a year, or longer?
Is it one who is born with faith and joy? Furthermore, one should weigh the gravity of the offenses to be extinguished:

a single thought-moment extinguishes the heavy sins of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas—those heavy sins being shedding the Buddha’s blood, causing a schism in the Saṃgha, killing an Arhat, killing one’s father, and killing one’s mother. By reciting the name of the Buddha for a single thought-moment, these are extinguished.

If the destruction of sins is thus, how much more so the sins destroyed by ten recitations? How much more so the sins destroyed by reciting the Buddha’s name for one day, one month, one year, or even one lifetime?
Even grave transgressions are extinguished; how much more so minor offenses?

Furthermore, one should compare the merit of reciting the Buddha’s name with other roots of goodness to discern their relative superiority and inferiority. As a sutra says: "If a person were to provide the four requisites..."

The merit obtained by making offerings of the most excellent things to fill the great trichiliocosm with Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas is not equal to that of a person who joins their palms once and recites "Namo Buddhāya" once. Compared to the merit of those holy ones in the great trichiliocosm,
even if one were to divide it into a hundredth part, a thousandth part, or a hundred-thousand-billionth part, or describe it through calculation and analogy, it would still be insufficient.

It cannot be compared. The merit of one who utters the name of the Buddha once is immeasurable. If the merit of uttering the name of the Buddha once is already such, how much more so for one who recollects the Buddha ten times?
How much more so for the merit obtained by those who recollect Amitābha Buddha for a day, a month, a year, or for their entire life?
Furthermore, it should be known that those who practice the recollection of the Buddha will enjoy peace and security in the present life; all the sages...

Guard yourselves. Stay far from all calamities and misfortunes. To speak briefly by way of comparison: in the customs of the present age, people vie with one another in sacrificing to ghosts and spirits, seeking their blessings and hoping for peace and security.
Yet they believe in the heterodox and take the lives of living beings; thus they create sin and bind themselves in enmity. There will certainly be no auspicious fortune that can benefit others;
instead, they vainly invite the retribution of hell in their future lives. As the *I Ching* says: "In a family that accumulates non-goodness, there will surely be a surplus [of calamity]."
Calamity. To kill living beings and harm their lives, following ancestral sacrificial rites that have not been established for but a morning or an evening—is this not the accumulation of non-virtue?

How can one doubt that such acts bring about retribution? If you claim that killing is not non-virtuous, why is it that throughout antiquity and the present, emperors and kings have transformed the world through benevolence and compassion, overcoming violence and abolishing slaughter?
Why do they allow birds and fish to follow their natures and lead all beings into the realm of longevity, universally extolling such conduct as virtuous? Indeed...
Regarding the methods of sacrifice—the Vedas of India and the sacrificial canons of China—they have not escaped worldly discourse; they are merely expedient means for guiding the mundane.
Although the Duke of Zhou is praised for serving the spirits, he did not comprehend the Way of the collective response of Heaven and Earth. How could Confucius have been able to serve ghosts?
He was simply deluded regarding the source of the six realms of existence. Since the scriptures of Laozi were already conflated with the Nine Schools, Zhuangzi likewise failed to shift [the course].
Among the hundred schools of thought, it is only the Buddhist tradition that exhaustively elucidates these principles. The celestial realm is situated above;
humanity occupies the next level; the asuras dwell in the middle; and ghosts and animals are below. Now, to serve a deity by means of human affairs is like bowing one’s head to another’s feet.

Furthermore, it is like a sovereign serving his subjects—how extreme is such perversity! Moreover, ghosts possess perverse powers; if one serves them for a long time, they will surely gather their own kind.

[Beings] of such a kind die and fall into it. How deluded the world is! Furthermore, the Great Master of the Three Realms, the Compassionate Father of myriad virtues—those who take refuge in him have their sins extinguished, and those who revere him give rise to blessings. This is fully explained in the various sutras.

If one can even briefly take refuge in the Triple Gem and uphold the name of a single Buddha, one shall obtain ten kinds of benefits in this present life. First, day and night one shall constantly obtain all...
First, the great powerful divine generals of the various heavens, with retinues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, will protect them by concealing their forms.
Second, they will constantly be followed and protected by twenty-five great bodhisattvas, such as Avalokiteśvara and others, as well as all other bodhisattvas.
Third, they will always be protected and mindful of by all Buddhas day and night; Amitābha Buddha will constantly emit light to gather this person under his care.
Fourth, none of the various evil spirits—whether yakṣas or rākṣasas—will be able to harm them; no venomous snakes, poisonous dragons, or toxic drugs will have any effect upon them.
Fifth, they shall be free from all calamities of fire or water, as well as from enemies, bandits, swords, and arrows.
Sixth, they shall not suffer imprisonment, shackles, or fetters, nor shall they undergo violent or unjust deaths;

all previously committed sins shall be completely extinguished, and the life-forces of those they have killed shall attain liberation, so that no further retribution or opposition remains. Seventh, their dreams at night shall be upright and clear.
Or again, one may dream of Amitābha Buddha, with his supreme and wondrous form and appearance. Eighth, the mind is constantly joyful;
the complexion is radiant and lustrous; physical strength is abundant; and all undertakings are auspicious.
Ninth, one is constantly honored and provided for by all the people of the world, who joyfully prostrate before them as if honoring a Buddha. Tenth, at the time of death, the mind is free from...
Free from fear, with right mindfulness and joy, one will manifestly behold Amitābha Buddha and the assembly of holy ones.
Holding a golden lotus pedestal, they will be welcomed and led to rebirth in the Western Pure Land, where they shall enjoy supreme and wondrous bliss until the end of the future.

O wise people, consider the benefits and merits obtained in this present life through the practice of *nianfo* (recollection of the Buddha); how could these ever be equal to the sacrificial rites of worldly men?
...of this Dharma. Will there not be no benefit or merit in the present, and suffering in the future?
Furthermore, one must have faith that all Mahāyāna sūtras praise the adornment of the Western Pure Land and exhort one to be reborn there.

Whether it be the *Avataṃsaka*, the Vaipulya, the *Prajñāpāramitā*, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, or the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*—all these various sections and sūtras demonstrate the modes of practice and extol their merits. Moreover, as for the bodhisattvas...

Both Vasubandhu and Nāgārjuna each composed treatises in praise of the Pure Land. Furthermore, various Dharma masters and Chan masters of this land have each written treatises and commentaries to glorify the Western Paradise:
Master Dao’an’s *Wangsheng lun* (Treatise on Rebirth) in ten fascicles; Master Huiyuan’s *Quan jing shu* (Commentary on the Sutra of Exhortation) in one fascicle;
and Master Zhizhe of Tiantai’s *Shi yi lun* (Treatise on the Ten Doubts) and *Guanjing shu* (Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra).
There is one fascicle each of commentaries on the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*. Master Daochuo composed the three-fascicle *Anleji* (*Collection on Peace and Bliss*).

Upādhyāya Shandao established the Five-Assembly Teaching to exhort people to practice nianfo; he also composed one fascicle of commentary on the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra*, as well as one fascicle each of the *Twenty-four Praises* and the *Text for the Six Periods of Liturgy*.
Dharma Master Huigan attained the samādhi of nianfo and composed the seven-fascicle *Jueyi lun* (*Treatise on Resolving Doubts*).
The Tripitaka Master Cimin compiled the *Jingtu Cibei Ji* (Anthology on the Compassion of the Pure Land) in three fascicles;
Dharma Master Ci'en composed the *Amitābha Sūtra Commentary* in two fascicles; and the State-Protecting Śramaṇa Chengguan composed the *Contemplation Sūtra Commentary* in one fascicle.

Upon hearing of these, who would not believe and rejoice in them, as the various sages praise and exhort others toward rebirth therein? Save for those unworthy persons who are deluded, blind, and devoid of wisdom.
Furthermore, this work cites from ancient times to the present day thirty-three instances of manifest verification concerning the往生 (ōjō) of eminent individuals— monastics and laypeople,
men and women— from India and China. It is presented in full for the sake of future generations, with the hope that all worthy and accomplished persons will together aspire to be born there.
The Verse on Establishing Right Faith in Rebirth Based on the Sūtras:

(If one can recite and uphold this verse, one shall obtain three kinds of benefits: first, one will always be able to hold the titles of the names of all Mahāyāna sūtras; second, one will increase one’s faith in the Pure Land; third, those who hear it will develop deep faith in the Pure Land.)
If you encounter one who is approaching the end of life, recite [the name] aloud once or twice, and then encourage them to practice mindfulness of the Buddha.
Bowing my head to the World-Honored One of Great Compassion, Amitābha, in the Western Land of Peace and Bliss,
I have, relying upon various sūtras, achieved the resolute faith of rebirth there.
Those who abide in the Mahāyāna possess a pure mind; by recollecting that Amitāyus ten times, they will surely be reborn there at the end of life, having dreamed of the Buddha.
Thus it is said in the *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*.
The fires of the five heinous offenses appear in hell; yet, upon meeting a virtuous friend, one arouses a fierce resolve. By reciting the Buddha’s name ten times, one is immediately reborn there.
Thus it is said in the *Sutra of the Sixteen Contemplations*.
If one possesses a heart of joy, faith, and delight, even ten recitations will lead to rebirth there; were it otherwise, Buddhahood would not be achieved.
Thus it is stated in the Forty-Eight Vows.

"Whoever hears this name and gives rise to a sincere mind, by dedicating even a single thought toward rebirth, shall attain birth there. This excludes only those who commit the five heinous crimes or slander the True Dharma.
Thus it is said in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*.

At the time of death, one may be unable to practice contemplation or recitation; yet, if one simply forms the thought of knowing that the Buddha exists, this person will be reborn in the Pure Land immediately upon the cessation of breath.
The *Mahābherī-haraka-parivarta Sūtra* speaks thus.

If one suspends silk banners and canopies for a single day and night, maintaining a focused mind on rebirth without interruption, one will dream of the Buddha while lying down and attain rebirth immediately;
thus it is said in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*.
Reciting the Buddha’s name day and night for one full day, with diligent and uninterrupted perseverance, exhorting one another in turn to be reborn together—
thus it is said in the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra*.
Whether for one day, two days, or seven days, if one holds fast to the name with an undistracted mind, the Buddha will appear before them and they shall attain rebirth there;
thus it is said in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*.
"If a person hears of that Amitābha for one day, two days, or even longer, and maintains focused mindfulness before them, they will immediately attain rebirth there.
Thus it is said in the Pratyutpanna Sūtra."

For ten days and ten nights, during the six periods of the day and night, one should prostrate with the five limbs before the Buddha and maintain uninterrupted mindfulness; thus one will see that Buddha face-to-face and attain rebirth there.
The *Drum-Sound King Sūtra* (*Ghoṣadattarāja-sūtra*) speaks thus.

For ten days and ten nights, observe the fast and precepts; hang silk banners and canopies, and burn incense and lamps. By maintaining constant mindfulness without interruption, one shall attain rebirth there.
Thus it is said in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*.
If a person single-mindedly contemplates a Buddha of one direction for seven weeks, whether walking or sitting, they shall see that Buddha in their present body and be reborn there;
thus it is said in the Mahāsannipāta Sūtra.
If a person vows to practice constant walking meditation for ninety days, neither sitting nor lying down, they will see Amitābha Buddha within samādhi;
thus it is stated in the established scriptures.
If a person sits upright facing due west and constantly recollects the Buddha for ninety days, they will be able to achieve samādhi and be born before the Buddha;
thus it is said in the Mañjuśrī-prajñā-sūtra.
Regarding a small portion of the verses from the various sūtras, even if I were to speak in this manner, there would be no end. May those who hear this together give rise to right faith;
the Buddha’s words are true and free from deception.

A doubter asks: "Observing this verse, there are ten levels of mindfulness; even those who give rise to a single thought of faith and joy, or even those who merely form the intention of knowing that the Buddha exists, will be born in that land.
Furthermore, it is said that one must practice mindfulness of the Buddha for seven times seven days, up to ninety days, before one can attain birth there.
Since the Pure Land is one and the same, why do the causes cultivated differ so drastically? The explanation states: Regarding the Pure Land...

Although the soil is one, those who grow within it differ from one another. The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* categorizes them into three grades in total, while the *Sixteen Contemplations Sūtra* opens this into nine grades;

if further subdivided, they would indeed be immeasurable. Furthermore, a doubt is raised: since the causes cultivated by those of the lower grades are shallow, they ought to experience regression and fall.
The explanation says: this is not so. Having attained the nine grades, there are differences in the speed with which their lotuses bloom and they approach the Buddha.

There are distinctions of distance and proximity; there are differences in the sharpness or dullness of those who attain the Way. Yet, as for those born there, all are by rule non-retrogressive. As the Sūtra says:
"Those who are born there all abide in the assembly of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*). It further states: "All sentient beings who are born there are *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive)."
This refers to non-retrogression. In the *Ten Doubts Treatise*, it is stated that there are five causes and conditions for non-retrogression:

first, because one is sustained by the power of Amitābha Buddha’s great compassionate vows; second, because the Buddha’s light constantly shines upon them, their bodhicitta constantly increases and does not regress;
third, because the waterfowl, trees, forests, and the sounds of the wind and music all proclaim suffering and emptiness.
First, because those who hear [the teaching] constantly give rise to the mind that recollects the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, they do not regress.

Second, those dull-witted bodhisattvas in that land take them as virtuous friends; there are no objects of adverse conditions, no external ghosts, spirits, or demons, and internally there are no afflictions such as the three poisons, so that afflictions never arise at all, and thus they do not regress. Fifth, upon being born in that land, their lifespan is eternal.
In kalpas past, because they were equal to Bodhisattvas and Buddhas, they did not regress; how much more so in this degenerate age?

Not only are these five conditions lacking, but furthermore, there are evil friends and associates, intoxication by sounds and forms, demons and ghosts masquerading as the true, and a short lifespan—all five of these being evil, obstructing and vexing the cultivation of the Way, such that vast kalpas pass in vain. I pray you reflect deeply upon this; I pray you reflect deeply upon this.

Someone says: "All phenomena are fundamentally without arising or ceasing; they are equal, empty, and quiescent. Why then do you insist on urging others to abandon this and seek that? The commentary states:

If you claim that seeking rebirth in the Western Land constitutes a process of grasping and rejecting, thereby contradicting the principle of equality, then you yourself are merely rejecting that [Western Land] while clinging to this [this world].
Is this not likewise a contradiction of reason? If you further argue: "I also do not seek rebirth..."
If one were to seek birth even here, that would constitute the nihilistic view of annihilation (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*). Does the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* not discourse on emptiness?
The Buddha cautioned Subhūti, saying: "Do not harbor such a thought; those who have resolved upon bodhicitta do not speak of the characteristic of annihilation regarding phenomena.
One who truly understands emptiness realizes, within the very context of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), that arising is non-arising.
The nature [of things] is the nature of cessation and non-cessation; it does not mean annihilation or non-existence, but rather that they are neither born nor extinguished.

The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "Of those phenomena produced by causes and conditions, I say they are empty. This does not mean that they become empty only after being extinguished and ceased. The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra* says:
"Though he knows that all Buddha-lands and sentient beings are empty, he constantly cultivates pure lands and teaches and transforms all living beings. Someone may ask:
"The Pure Land resides within the mind; why seek it externally? As the mind becomes pure, so does the Buddha-land become pure.
Why then go to such great lengths to seek rebirth in a Pure Land in another direction? The commentary states: "You, moreover, do not well understand the meaning of the 'mind-land.

You seem to think that my mind is confined to the space of an inch square, and thus you perceive the West as being situated far beyond the realm. If this were the case, then [your objection] would hold; however..."
Why is it said that when the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure? The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "The mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction.
Since the Buddha-dharma is all-pervasive, the dharma of the mind is likewise all-pervasive. If each possessed its own distinct direction, how could they be said to be without distinction?

Furthermore, it says: "The mind wanders through the Dharma-realm as if through empty space. How could there be any partition within empty space? If one realizes that a single thought-moment pervades all, [the Buddha-land is pure].
Even a single mote of dust pervades hundreds of thousands of billions of lands; how could that which lies within the span of a few steps exist outside of the mind?
If worldly people speak of the principle of emptiness, they dismiss cause and effect; if they speak of their own mind, they do not believe in the existence of external phenomena.

This is not only a slander of the Dharma, but also a slander of one's own mind, leading to calamities that fall for ten thousand kalpas—how truly lamentable! To falsely create right and wrong is to obstruct others.
The Pure Land is truly a false spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). The *Sūtra of Immeasurable Life* states: The Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva:
"O devas and humans, in the land of Immeasurable Life, the merit and wisdom of the śrāvakas and bodhisattvas are beyond description.
Furthermore, that land is so subtle, peaceful, and pure as this. Why do you not strive to do good? Contemplate the spontaneity of the Way."
Each of you should diligently apply yourselves with vigor; strive to seek this for yourselves. You will surely attain transcendence and be reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss.
You shall cross over the five evil paths, and those evil paths will naturally close. The ascending path is infinite and boundless; it is easy to travel, yet few do so.
In that land there is no opposition; one is naturally drawn [there]. Why not abandon worldly affairs and diligently practice to seek the Way and its Virtue?
Thus one may attain ultimate longevity, with life and bliss without end.
In the *Hymn to the Buddha* by Śīlabhadra of the Avataṃsaka, it is further said:
"There is a radiance named 'Beholding the Buddha. This light awakens those whose end is near, causing them to see the Tathāgata through recollection;
upon the end of their life, they attain birth in that Pure Land."

Seeing those at the point of death, they exhort them to recite the Buddha’s name and show them sacred images to behold and revere, thereby causing them to develop deep faith and aspiration toward the Buddha;
for this reason, they attain this radiance.
Regarding these two verses: the first four lines praise the Buddha’s emission of light, which is called "Seeing the Buddha" (darśana-buddha).
It enables those facing death to see the Buddha and attain rebirth [in the Pure Land]. The latter four lines praise the causes through which the Buddha cultivated this radiance. As for those causes:
This was merely to exhort those facing death to recite the Buddha’s name and to show them an image of the Buddha; thus, when they attain Buddhahood, they obtain this radiance.
Now, in widely distributing these verses, I aim to encourage those with deep faith, so that whenever they encounter their kin or any other person, [they may likewise be inspired].
At the time of death, one must ensure that a Buddha image placed before the bed is within the person's sight and encourage them to recite the Buddha’s name.

Even if they are oppressed by intense pain, or if they previously lacked faith and are unwilling to recite the Buddha’s name, one must still employ various skillful means to urge them to invoke the Buddha’s name.
By doing so for even as few as ten recitations, one can extinguish heavy karmic offenses and be reborn in the Buddha’s Pure Land. This is the first [point].
The benefit is inconceivable. If one can exhort even a single person to be born in the Pure Land, then even if one does not practice oneself, one is still destined to be born in the Buddha-land;
how much more so when one will later attain Buddhahood and be able to emit radiance that illuminates all sentient beings, allowing them to see the Buddha at the moment of death.
One often sees people of the world who, for the sake of affection and attachment, gather together to wail and weep, without considering how to save and deliver one another.
Alas, alas! These are called evil associates. Drawn by the bonds of affection, one falls into the evil realms with no prospect of liberation.
There are five kinds of people in the world who are unwilling to practice mindfulness of the Buddha: first, those who originally lack faith; second, those who are attached to wealth and treasures;
third, those who cannot abandon their wives and children; fourth, those who cherish their own bodies and lives; and fifth, those burdened by sinful karma.
Obstructed by these, one falls into hell at death. May you awaken to this quickly!
In the Preface to the General Praise of the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, Master Ci'en explains in detail:
"The principle transcends all verbal designations; how could it be encompassed by the Three Vehicles? Wisdom is perfected in myriad virtues; it is not [attained] by the Ten Stages."
He was able to contemplate: spreading the clouds of compassion to shelter the four modes of birth, and showering the rain of Dharma to nourish the nine realms of existence.
Thus, he descended his spirit from Tuṣita Heaven and manifested his traces in Kapilavastu. He grew weary of sensual pleasures in the royal palace and attained true permanence beneath the Bodhi tree.

This was truly because the karmic delusions of sentient beings were so vast and the factions of Māra were so powerful that he crossed the sea of suffering to open the way for the three paths, and boarded the boat of compassion to swallow up [the world].

Thus, the myriad virtues are perfected. For this reason, the net of the Teaching is loftily spread, directly pointing toward the Pure Land. This is the profound gateway for entering the state of sagehood and the wondrous path for transcending the mundane world.

The ten grades of the Pure Land are differentiated according to the stages of spiritual attainment (*bhūmi*), while the nine ranks of the lotus pedestals correspond to the sequence of one's faculties and dispositions.
How magnificent! It casts far beyond the gates of emptiness and existence, uniquely excelling above the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism. The Buddha...

"Enlightened One" (*Buddha*) refers to one whose realization of the Path is already perfected. "Speaker" (*bhāṣita*) refers to the preaching of the Dharma with a compassionate mind. "Amitābha" means Immeasurable Life.

"Sūtra" (*sūtra*) refers to the constant Dharma that threads together and encompasses all teachings. "Constant" implies that it is not altered by a hundred kings; "Dharma" implies that it shares the same standard for a thousand generations;

"encompassing" implies including all modes of expression; and "threading" implies penetrating the subtle principles. Therefore, it is called the *Buddhabhāṣitāmitābhasūtra* (The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on Amitābha).
Preface to the Commentary on the Meaning of the *Amitābha Sūtra* by Master Gushan:
As for the essence of the nature of mind, it is luminous and quiescent; it is simply one. It is devoid of ordinary beings and sages;
devoid of the dependent and the primary [realms]; devoid of extension and brevity; and devoid of purity and defilement. Yet, when it responds to objects and transforms according to conditions, then—
There are the six classes of ordinary beings and the four types of noble ones. There is the dependent [environment] and there is the primary [body].

Once the dependent and the primary have been established, then lifespans vary in their extension or brevity, and lands vary in their purity or defilement. Our Buddha, the Great Sage, attained the essence of clarity and stillness;
he took the path of loving-kindness as his vehicle and made compassion his dwelling place, intending to lead the masses of deluded beings back to their original state.
Fundamentally, herein lies the principle: though without a body, one manifests a body; though without a land, one manifests a land.

One prolongs their lifespan and purifies their land to inspire joy, or shortens their lifespan and defiles their land to incite weariness. Once they are both joyful and weary, the strategy of gradual induction succeeds.
Therefore, when Śākyamuni manifested a limited lifespan and took up a defiled land, was it not because he desired to incite weariness? Maitreya...
The Tathāgata manifests immeasurable purity to take up a pure land; is it not because he desires others to rejoice in it?
This is to subdue them, while that is to gather them in, so as to cause them to return to their original state and realize their nature.

Thus, when the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra says, "One takes up a Buddha-land according to how one tames sentient beings," is this not precisely what is meant? Although jeweled towers and golden ponds serve as objects of delight for the eyes, [they are but expedients].
Without the colors that delude and disperse the mind, one is able to realize that there is only mind and no external objects.

Although the sounds of wind in the trees and birds have the pleasure of entering the ears, they are not discordant or jarring tones; yet through them, one is able to maintain mindfulness of the Three Jewels as one’s refuge.
If one acts in this manner, returning to the essence of luminous stillness is like turning over one’s palm. As the Sūtra says: "All those born among sentient beings are..."
This refers to the *Avivartika* (the non-retrogressive). How magnificent! Such is the skillful means (*upāya*) of the Sage.

Therefore, although the various scriptures are arrayed in abundance, they all specifically extol the Pure Land; how profound their intent is! When the Buddha preached the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, was it not precisely this specific extolling?
I cherish its phrasing for being concise yet clear in principle, and its prose for being succinct yet comprehensive in detail. It is sufficient...

This may serve to guide those who are weak and lost, and to strike at the ignorance of the young and simple. Thus, I have summarized the school of Nāgārjuna and followed the teachings of the Wise One (Zhiyi).

Relying upon the sūtras to discern the principles, I have composed this commentary on the meaning. As for fathoming the utmost depths and investigating the subtle nuances, how could I presume to do so?
My hope is merely that it may assist the true tradition and provide benefit for future generations.

In the *Yuanzhongchao* (Excerpts on the Perfect [Meaning] of the Amitābha Sūtra), Master Youxi states that when the response bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) of all Buddhas interact with sentient beings, there are four kinds of benefit: first, benefit through form, which is the manifestation of the body;

second, benefit through light, which is the emission of radiance; third, benefit through sound, which is the preaching of the Dharma; and fourth, benefit through supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), which is the manifestation of...
This is the divine power (ṛddhipāda). It is solely through Amida that, beyond the four ways of benefiting others, one further adds the reception of beings by means of his Name;

this is because he possesses the vows he originally made. The other four ways of reception have a narrow scope for gathering sentient beings, whereas receiving beings solely by means of the Name has a vast scope for gathering them. Since Amida receives beings by means of the Name, sentient beings—
Having been able to hear it with my ears and recite it with my mouth, how could it be merely a single invocation of a sublime title? Rather, ten thousand virtues are simultaneously manifested.
Furthermore, boundless sagely merits are gathered into the conscious mind, becoming forever the seed of Buddhahood; eradicating sins and realizing the Way—this is inconceivable.
How could the merit of these roots of goodness be considered minor? I humbly examine the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land: that which it reveals is one and the same.
Although the methods of cultivation differ and its gates are many, when one examines their ultimate destination, they do not exceed two types:

first, the primary cultivation (*samyak-prayoga*); second, the auxiliary practices (*upāya-caryā*). Within the primary cultivation, there are two methods: first, visualization (*bhāvanā*); second, the recitation of the name (*nāmadheya-dhāraṇa*).
If one focuses the mind on visualization, the text is found in the *Contemplation Sūtra*. If one focuses the mind on the recitation of the name, the text is found in this sūtra.

If visualization and the recitation of the name are practiced together, the text is found in the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra*. Now, if we wish to clarify their meanings, there are five points of difference.
First, the names and the realities differ. "Name" refers to the provisional designation within the Buddha-realm; as for "reality," it is...

Regarding the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of the Buddha-realm and its land: if one contemplates the real dharmas of the five aggregates, one contemplates the nine contemplations shown in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra*, such as the three grades of rebirth for Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
if one contemplates the land as the supported retribution (*niśraya-vipāka*), one contemplates the six contemplations shown in the same sūtra, such as the sun, ice, earth, and trees.
Furthermore, according to what is shown in the *Pratyutpanna-samādhi-sūtra*, one simply contemplates the real dharmas of the Buddha’s body as the primary retribution (*mukhya-vipāka*).

Thus it is. What is shown in the present sutra is that one merely maintains the provisional name; therefore, it says, "Upon hearing the teaching of Amitābha Buddha, one should grasp and maintain his name.
This is to practice according to this sutra by taking the six-syllable sound of the Buddha’s name as the object of focus (*ālambana*).

One does not employ the visualization of the Buddha’s physical marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), lest it confuse the essential purport of the sutra. As it is said: "A single recitation of this auspicious name [eradicates] ten thousand..."

Virtues are equally manifested; by citing provisional names, the ultimate reality is fully encompassed. Thus, one knows that what is shown in this sutra is a dharma-gate that grasps the main principles and the essential points.
Second, regarding the difference between the relaxed and the urgent, such as the sixteen sublime contemplations shown in the *Amitābha Sūtra*.

When first practicing the visualization of the sun, one must wait for its accomplishment before changing the visualization to the water, the ice, and so forth, progressing slowly and steadily until it is perfected within a single lifetime.
The method of holding the name shown in this sutra extends to a maximum period of seven days;
subsequently, one may hold the name for six, five, or even down to a single day, maintaining single-mindedness without distraction. Furthermore, [the text continues:]
The *Amitābha Sūtra* teaches that those of the lower grade attain rebirth, while the *Great Amitābha Sūtra* states that one attains rebirth through ten recitations at the moment of death.
Thus, we know that what this [latter] sūtra demonstrates is a dharma-gate that excels in urgency over slowness. Third, the difficulties and ease differ:

the *Contemplation Sūtra* instructs on meditative visualization because the mental faculties of ordinary beings are weak and inferior; therefore, it first shows the visualization of the sun facing west to provide a point of focus.
As for that mind: wait until the mind has become still and subtle, and then contemplate water and ice, up to the accomplishment of the contemplation of the image;

only then should one contemplate the Buddha’s true body (*dharmakāya*). This must be practiced by those whose faculties have been matured through long-term cultivation. This is what is shown in the present sutra.
Ordinary beings at the initial stage of the path may simply have the mouth to recite and the faith to contemplate; thus, all are capable of practicing this.
Therefore, one should know that the Dharma-gate revealed in this sutra is a method so concise and easy to access. Regarding the four distinct types of pure lands and the sixteen contemplation gates:

for those at the initial stage who practice them, they must enter meditative concentration (*samādhi*) in the full-lotus posture before they can perform the contemplations. Once they emerge from concentration and encounter the conditions of daily life, these [contemplations] are not applicable.
Regarding the scope: if one upholds the Name, it may be practiced whether one is free from or beset by busyness, regardless of whether one is active or still;

it may be cultivated while walking, standing, sitting, or lying down. Thus, one knows that this sutra reveals a dharma-gate that is swift and direct. Fifth, the difference in the capacity of those to be gathered:
if one practices according to the *Contemplation Sutra*, it only reaches those of superior faculties; therefore, the capacity for such practice is narrow.
It is not restricted. The method of invoking the Name makes no distinction between the wise and the foolish, nor does it select between men and women.
Whether poor or rich, whether noble or lowly, all may practice it. Thus we know that what this sutra demonstrates is a dharma-gate that encompasses sentient beings with the utmost breadth.
Therefore, the objective realm and contemplation clarified in this sutra need only concern the single act of upholding the Name as the object of contemplation.

Regarding the objects—whether phenomena or principles—all are explained and cultivated by means of this alone; there is no need to further rely on the contemplation of the Buddha’s physical marks and signs as a supplementary addition.
The *Sūtra on the Method of Holding the Name* states: "If there are good men or good women who, upon hearing the teaching of Amitābha Buddha,
uphold his name— whether for one day, two days, three days, four days, five days, six days, or seven days..."
"One day with single-mindedness and without distraction. A brief commentary states: "Grasping" (執) means to take hold of; "maintaining" (持) means to sustain.
By the power of faith, one takes hold of [the practice] within the mind; by the power of mindfulness, one sustains it without forgetting. "If" is an indefinite term.

Those of sharp faculties may achieve success in a single day and a single thought, while those of dull faculties may require up to seven weeks for the practice to be perfected. Even if they have not yet destroyed their delusions, they are certain to attain rebirth.
The cause is single-mindedness without distraction. This consists of both the phenomenal and the noumenal. Regarding single-mindedness of phenomena (*dharma-ekāgratā*):

the practitioner binds their attention to the mindfulness of Amitābha Buddha’s physical marks, signs, and radiance, without any intention to disperse it, maintaining continuity from moment to moment; this is called single-mindedness of phenomena. Regarding single-mindedness of principle (*tattva-ekāgratā*):
one thoroughly realizes that both the mind that recollects and the Buddha who is recollected are devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Although they are originally...
Emptiness and quiescence interact through the Way of resonance, like reflections in a mirror or the moon in water, spontaneously manifesting benefit. At their very locus they are entirely empty;

as a whole, they are provisionally existent. Neither of the two extremes can be found, and even the Middle Way does not exist. The three truths are perfectly interfused, transcending thought and beyond discourse.
This is called the "single mind of principle. One must thoroughly comprehend that the Dharma-realm is mind-only and that there are no objects external to the mind.

Amitābha’s physical marks and signs are originally one's own mind; the ten million billion lands do not transcend the present thought-moment, because all phenomena are inherently possessed by nature and are not obtained from another.

The *Yuanzhong chao* states: "The passage 'thoroughly comprehending' below clarifies the meaning of 'immediate emptiness. It means that both the subject who recollects and the object recollected are both devoid of self-nature."

Regarding "nature" (*svabhāva*): this refers to the four natures, through which one realizes that the essence is unborn. One should say that there is also no "other-nature," "common nature," or "causeless nature";
these are omitted from the text. Herein, it is appropriate to take the fact that the mind capable of mindfulness is fundamentally empty as being the absence of self-nature;

and that Amitābha, the object of mindfulness, is fundamentally empty as being the absence of other-nature. The mutual resonance of cause and response is like a reflection in a mirror or the moon in water.
It is not of the nature of being causeless, for it spontaneously manifests benefit; this is to subsume the latter into the former in order to clarify that there are no four natures.
Next, from "Although originally empty and quiescent" onwards, it clarifies the conventional (the provisional). The first two lines clarify the conventionality in terms of phenomena (*dharma*);
the latter two lines clarify the conventionality in terms of analogy. This uses the form and the water as analogies for the response, and the mirror...
This corresponds to the analogy of the moon and its reflection. The moon in the mirror has no intentionality, yet it naturally manifests its image;
the water likewise has no purpose, yet it spontaneously responds to the moon in the mirror. When this merit reaches the point of rebirth, benefits are revealed through effortless spontaneity.

That which is empty in its very place means that existence is itself emptiness. That the whole body is itself provisional means that emptiness is itself existence. Since existence is itself emptiness, then...
Existence is itself non-existence; emptiness is itself existence, and thus emptiness is itself non-emptiness. When there is neither emptiness nor existence, the Middle Way is manifest.
When there is both emptiness and existence, even the Middle Way perishes. Therefore it is said: "The two extremes cannot be grasped, and the Middle Way does not exist."
Thus, the objects of contemplation are the three truths in perfect fusion; the contemplating mind is beyond thought and beyond discourse.

The two gates of phenomena and principle have already been briefly indicated in the section on interpretation. If one wishes to further clarify their essential meaning, there are two different types: the horizontal and the vertical.
Regarding the horizontal discussion of the three contemplations, that which contemplates belongs to the three contemplations, while that which is contemplated belongs to the three [truths].
Contemplate thus: at the very moment one correctly utters a name, the mind that performs the utterance is understood to be neither internal nor external, formless and without characteristics;

this is the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Although it lacks internal or external form, this mindful mind is vividly and clearly manifest; this is the contemplation of the provisional (*prajñapti*).
Yet, this mindfulness does not exist apart from the provisional, nor does the provisional exist apart from emptiness; both are simultaneously negated and simultaneously affirmed.
Illumination is itself the Middle Way. The names of the Buddha and his vocal sounds are like echoes in a valley or the moon reflected in water;
they are utterly ungraspable, which is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Although they are ungraspable, the name and sound of the Buddha are nonetheless clearly present in the mouth.

It is evident that what is heard with the ears is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Furthermore, this object of contemplation does not exist apart from the ultimate, nor does the ultimate exist apart from the conventional;
their simultaneous presence and simultaneous forgetting constitute the middle truth (*madhyama-satya*). This is the horizontal exposition of the three contemplations and the three truths.
If one explains this vertically: taking "a single mind free from distraction and all conditions simultaneously stilled" as the contemplation of emptiness;

and taking "the six-syllable sacred name being recited with clear and distinct resonance" as the contemplation of the provisional. Although the faculty that recites is empty, the reciter is vividly present;
although the object recited is provisional, it is like an echo and lacks substantial reality. Thus, it is both empty and not empty, yet it is empty.

It is precisely the provisional; it is precisely the provisional yet not the provisional. Yet the provisional is itself emptiness. Both are negated and both are illumined; subject and object, as well as contemplation, are both forgotten.

That which is called the "provisional" refers to the wondrous provisional, and that which is called "emptiness" refers to contemplation. When subject and object, as well as contemplation, are both forgotten, this is the Middle Way.

How could there ever be a sequence between forgetting and illumination? Within the single mind, all is fused and severed, leaving no trace whatsoever. If this is so, then those who seek rebirth in the Pure Land need only, with a single...
The mind is undistracted while upholding the Name; by merely upholding the Name, the mind is single-mindedly undistracted.
Within this lies the entirety of boundless, wondrous meaning. This inconceivable contemplation is not separate from its own essence; it may be called the arising of cultivation entirely from nature.
Complete cultivation resides within the nature.
Furthermore, one must understand the intended meaning of the sutra: "one mind without distraction" is intended to ensure that cause and effect correspond in name and substance;
"upholding the Name" is intended to ensure that the response between the living being and the Buddha intersects in the Way. Thus, cause and effect correspond in name and substance.

As for this, the Land of Ultimate Bliss is called the Pure Land. It is only when one’s own mind is pure that the Buddha-land becomes pure. Thus, the principle that "the mind being pure, the land is pure" is universally applicable.
Whether it be the complete subduing of the five abodes of ignorance or the complete destruction of the three delusions, all are termed "purity of mind.

When this purity of mind brings about the purity of the Buddha-land, it encompasses all four lands; however, the present case refers specifically to the Pure Land of Common Residence (*sahā-loka*). For this, one need only [practice] for a single day.
As for the seven days: holding fast to the Name with a single mind without distraction serves as the cause for rebirth through the purification of the mind.

Second, regarding the mutual resonance between the Buddha and sentient beings: Amitābha’s wondrous response is that of one who has already attained the fruit, and furthermore, he possesses his former vows.
It causes me to hold the name; therefore, one must necessarily grasp and maintain the Name as the cause for rebirth through mental purity.
Thus, "single-mindedness without distraction" and "grasping and maintaining the Name" are two meanings that require one another; it is not possible to lack either.

Consequently, the central tenet of this sutra must be analyzed through four propositions: first, single-mindedness that is not the grasping of the Name, which refers to the ordinary practice of dhyāna.
First, practicing various deeds with a single mind yet lacking dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) and the making of vows is entirely not the direct cause for rebirth there.

Second, holding the Name without a single mind—that is, holding the Name with a distracted mind—though it constitutes the causal seed for the Buddha Vehicle, is likewise not the direct cause for rebirth there.
Third, neither a single mind nor the holding of the Name—that is, the indolent ordinary person performing various good deeds.

Nor is it the cause for rebirth there. The fourth, which is single-mindedness (*ekacitta*) and the holding of the name (*nāmadheya-dhāraṇa*), is precisely the correct cause for rebirth as taught in this sutra.

If we consider this sutra—stated to belong to the Vaipulya (Vaipulya/ Fangdeng) and encompassing the capacities of the four teachings (*catur-yāna*)—and judge single-mindedness accordingly, there are four distinct types of practitioners:
1. The person of the *Āgama* (Tripitaka) Teaching: For them, the mind and the Buddha are substantially real; they judge [the practice] solely by way of phenomenal characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
The mind is not distracted; taking this as the cause, and further adding faith and aspiration, when the fruit ripens at the moment of death, one immediately attains rebirth.

As for ordinary people today who have not yet penetrated the ultimate principle, they merely shut off the six sense-faculties so that there is neither going out nor coming in, and single-mindedly hold the Name.

Or, they may apply their minds to investigate and analyze various aspects [of the practice]. These are all examples of those following the Tripitaka Teachings (Zangjiao) who single-mindedly hold the Name. (2)

As for those of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao), they are well able to penetrate and realize that whether it be the mind or the Buddha, both are like illusions and transformations. Since the Buddha is fundamentally non-existent, how could the mind exist?
Sounds are like echoes in a valley; the Buddha is like a reflection in a mirror. To understand and embody this in such a way is to realize non-arising in the very moment.

This is the single-minded holding of the name by those of the Shared Teaching. Third, as for those of the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao), they first are able to penetrate emptiness and are also able to penetrate the provisional.
Using my empty mind, I manifest a provisional Buddha; it is not only the Buddha who exists, for the mind likewise exists.

Yet, by using an empty mind to contemplate a provisional Buddha, emptiness is no longer empty and the provisional is no longer provisional. Being neither provisional nor empty, one perceives the Middle Way.

These are the practitioners of the Separate Teaching (*pratyeka-śāsana*), who single-mindedly hold the name.
