As for the practitioners of the Fourfold Perfect Teaching (*catur-yuganaddha-sampanna-śāsana*), they are able to realize that the Pure Land is mind-only and that Amitābha is one's own original nature.

Since both the ultimate and conventional truths, as well as emptiness and form within contemplation, are non-dual; and since whether there is mindfulness or no-mindfulness, there is nothing that is not the Dharma-nature;

and whether there is a Buddha or no Buddha, it is all True Suchness (*tathatā*); thus, throughout the day there is mindfulness and throughout the day there is no-mindfulness—this is the characteristic of mindfulness through non-mindfulness.
There is the characteristic of characteristics. Non-arising yet arising; arising yet non-arising. This refers to the person of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) who single-mindedly holds the Name.

This interpretation is according to the meaning of the Vaipulya (fangdeng) period. If one interprets it according to the *Lotus Sūtra*’s revelation of the Real by opening the Provisional, then all previous teachings should be harmonized and brought back to the Perfect and Sudden.
For those of the Tripitaka Teaching, they close off the six sense-faculties and restrain the mind from distraction for the sake of the self.
In the *Yuanjiao* (Perfect Teaching), the "one mind" within phenomena is the "one mind that is identical with emptiness" for me; in the *Tongjiao* (Common Teaching), it is like an illusion;
in the *Biejiao* (Distinct Teaching), it is transcending the mundane, which for me is the "one mind that is identical with the provisional.

Since the Perfect [Teaching] is fundamentally characterized by mutual identity, there is no need for reconciliation, because the *Lotus Sūtra* is subtle, possessing both kinds of subtlety. The previous "one mind" of the Perfect Teaching was the "subtlety" discussed through the *Lotus Sūtra*’s theory of relative comparison (*xiangdai*). Now, [this] unifies...
This is the ultimate convergence. It constitutes the *Lotus Sūtra*’s discourse on the "wondrous" (*miau*) as being absolutely without peer.

This is precisely the practitioner of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjia*), who has already heard the Wondrous Dharma and profoundly awakened to the Perfect Principle (*yuanli*). By giving rise to the Perfect School, such power and function are perfectly integrated and unimpeded:

phenomena are the principle itself, and the principle is the phenomena themselves. Therefore, when upholding the Name with a single mind, it is sufficient to maintain a single-mind focused on phenomena.

From the perspective of principle (*li*), it is sufficient to have one mind; from the perspective of phenomena (*shi*), principle and phenomena are mutually identical, so it is sufficient to have one mind.

Every thought-moment is nothing other than the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*); every mind is immediately the true and eternal. To practice *nien-fo* (Buddha-recollection) in this manner possesses the greatest merit:

it can subdue the afflictions of the five stages of dwelling, it can shatter the three delusions within the one mind, it can purify the four kinds of pure lands, and it enables one to behold Amitābha of the three bodies (*trikāya*). This is called [the practice of] non-...
This is contemplation through non-conceptualization; this is contemplation without effort (*anābhoga*). Yongming [Yanshou] said: "To have both Chan and Pure Land is like a tiger with horns;
in this life one serves as a teacher of men, and in future lives one becomes a Buddha or a Patriarch. This verse is precisely for those of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching.
This is the teaching for those who single-mindedly hold the Name.

The Dharma-realm has three meanings: first, the nature-endowment (*xingju*), which refers to the three thousand realms and ten dharma-realms; second, the nature-substance (*xingti*), which refers to the "pure and original" state, the True Suchness Dharma-realm;
third, the nature-capacity (*xingliang*), which refers to the one true Dharma-realm that vertically exhausts and horizontally pervades all things.

This refers to the extent of the universal realm (*dharmadhātu*). The nature of these three types of *dharmadhātu* is solely the discriminating consciousness of a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa-vikalpa-citta*) arising from the mutual correspondence between the sense organs and their objects.
Therefore, apart from the mind there is no object, and apart from the object there is no mind.

For this reason, the physical marks and signs of Amitābha are none other than the Amitābha of one’s own fundamental nature; the ten million billion lands are none other than the pure land of my own mind-only.

Therefore, it is said that the source is one's own mind; it does not transcend the present thought-moment. Thus, the conclusion states: "Because it is inherent in nature, it is not obtained from without.
The brief commentary says: Furthermore, one should know that Amitābha has already realized the ultimate First Noble Truth. To recite his name even once—

His title is such that ten thousand virtues are manifested all at once; sins are extinguished across kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, and blessings equal the void of space. How much more so for one day, let alone up to seven days!

This is truly due to the fundamental vows of Dharmakara: "If, when I attain Buddhahood, sentient beings of the ten directions who with sincere heart believe and rejoice, desiring to be born in my land, should fail to be reborn there even after ten recitations, may I not attain perfect enlightenment. Having already received the causal power of that Buddha’s vow—

The power of the intermediate vow results in radiance upon the attainment of fruition; holding the Name brings immeasurable merit, and one will certainly see the Buddha at the time of death without any doubt.

The *Yuanzhong chao* states: "In the previous explanation of 'one thought-moment' within the practice, it was spoken in reference to recollecting the Buddha’s physical marks, minor characteristics, and radiance, which seems to conflate with the *Contemplation Sūtra*, where the contemplation of the Buddha serves as the object of mindfulness. Although the application of the mind is the same, the objects being distinguished are different."

This is different. Now, it specifically points to the grasping and holding of the Name as the object of focus. Therefore, it is said: "Once the auspicious Name is invoked, the myriad virtues are simultaneously manifested.
This passage explains the latent doubts of certain individuals. Those who doubt say: "The Buddha possesses myriad virtues; one should contemplate his three bodies.
Why is it that merely invoking the Name allows one to attain rebirth? Thus, [the text] earnestly demonstrates this point.
It says: "Furthermore, one should know... and so forth. This passage explains the doubt by means of two points.
First, the correspondence between name and reality; second, the original vows of the Dharma-treasury. Regarding the first, the correspondence between name and reality, Siming states:
"Every single name of the fruit of perfect consummation is not in vain, but is ultimately accomplished. Indeed, all that is summoned [by these names] is the true ultimate."

Therefore, the Great Sūtra says: "In the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), there is only name but no actual reality; in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), there is both name and actual reality.

Since the Buddha is the ultimate ultimate truth, and since Amitābha has already realized this ultimate ultimate truth, the ten thousand virtues are simultaneously manifested by a single invocation of his auspicious name. Thus, Amitābha’s ten thousand virtues are like the sun of wisdom.

Since both the essence and the manifestation are equally revealed, the dark ignorance and karmic faults of sentient beings will naturally be extinguished within a single thought-moment, spanning aeons.
Once these karmic natures—which are fundamentally empty, void, and unreal—are eliminated, the merit and blessings equal to space will spontaneously arise from the power of chanting the Name.
If such is the case when the Name is chanted but once, how much more so when one chants it for one day up to seven days with a single-minded focus?
Even in times of chaos, if one upholds the Name, there is no transgression that will not be extinguished and no merit that will not arise.

At the time of death, one will be reborn in the Pure Land; this is certainly and without doubt not in vain. This is because, as stated below, the second section indicates the Original Vow of Dharmākara, and so forth.
Indeed, the Original Vows of all Buddhas are entirely free from falsehood, for Amitābha, while in the stage of a causal bodhisattva, made forty-eight vows.
Having completed these eight vows, he then traversed kalpas of eons in practice to fill the ocean of his vows.
Once the ocean of vows was full, immeasurable Dharma-treasures manifested all at once. Therefore, he has now taken up the Land of Ultimate Bliss to gather in sentient beings;

and since the beings of this Sahā world have already placed their faith in this matter, they continue to make the vow for rebirth therein, casting themselves into the ocean of vows, and further cultivate...

The practice of invoking the Name increases the mountain of conduct; as the ten thousand streams flow into the sea, they share one salty taste. As Mount Sumeru encompasses all things, they share one imperial-blue hue.
This occurs spontaneously and naturally, not through forced effort. Therefore, at the conclusion of the commentary on the text, the two meanings are unified to sever the root of doubt, stating:
"Having received the power of that Buddha’s vows during his causal stage and his radiance upon the fruition stage, one grasps..."
Holding the Name brings immeasurable merit; at the time of death, one will see the Buddha, of this there is no doubt.

Regarding the *Wusheng lun* (Treatise on Non-arising), the three contemplations are naturally capable of being contemplated as the three contemplations, and that which is contemplated is precisely the three truths. Because cultivation arises entirely from the inherent nature, it is called "natural" (*fa'er*).

The Treatise says: The three truths are the ultimate, the conventional, and the middle. The three contemplations are emptiness, the provisional, and the middle. Regarding the forgetting of emotions and the severing of conceptual understanding, nothing is superior to the ultimate.
Regarding responding to conditions through application, nothing is superior to the conventional. Regarding the harmonious integration of emptiness and existence, nothing is superior to the middle.
"Vast, spiritual, and unclouded: my mind is naturally empty. Objects come and it responds: my mind is naturally existent. Emptiness and existence are mutually identical:
my mind is naturally the mean. This is the nature, not cultivation; these are the three truths, not the three contemplations."

One who cultivates this refers to illuminating and comprehending it according to its true nature (*dharmatā*). To realize the substance of this mind as being void and devoid of all things is called "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*).

To illuminate and comprehend this nature as being fully endowed with the myriad phenomena is called "provisionality" (*prajñapti*). To harmonize these two extremes, being neither identical nor different, is called the "Middle Way" (*madhyamā pratipad*).

Thus, it is through this very emptiness and spiritual clarity that one responds to objects; it is through responding to objects that this emptiness and spiritual clarity is manifested. Emptiness is itself provisionality.

The Middle is [the same as] the provisional within emptiness; the Middle is [the same as] emptiness and the provisional. This is cultivation in accordance with the nature of reality; it is illumination that transcends all dependencies.
It is the inconceivable threefold contemplation (*trividha-vipaśyanā*), the compass for the Great Śūraṅgama Samādhi. Such is the detailed discussion. As for the general discussion:
some take the empty and numinous nature of one’s own mind to be emptiness, and the myriad phenomena observed therein to be...
The provisional (*prajñapti*). Taking the non-duality of mind and objects as the middle (*madhyama*). Objects are the objects of my own mind; how can they be provisional without being empty?

The mind is the mind of all phenomena; how can it be empty without being provisional? Mind is identical to objects, and objects are identical to mind. How can the middle be anything other than empty and provisional?
Therefore, when contemplating the environment and inhabitants of Sukhāvatī, one contemplates them with the single contemplation of one’s own mind—the three contemplations—illuminating them.
That there are three truths within that single object is not untenable; that one’s own mind of the three contemplations illuminates that single object of the three truths is likewise not untenable.
Master Huxi said: "The object is the wondrous provisional, and the contemplation is emptiness; when both object and contemplation are forgotten, this is the Middle Way.
How could forgetting and illumination ever have a sequence? Within the single mind, they are fused and transcendent. Thus it is fully understood.
Without trace, how could the three contemplations not conform to suchness?
In the Preface to the Commentary on the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra*, the Great Master Zhiyi [states]:
"The Land of Bliss and the realm of suffering; gold and jewels compared to silt and sand; the womb-hell in contrast to the Flower Pond; thorns..."

The forests compared to jade trees truly arise from the distinction between the defilement and purity of the mind; one perceives the rise and fall of the two lands through the opening of good and evil deeds, and the coarseness or subtlety of both regions.
This is like the analogy that when the form is upright, the shadow is straight, and when the source is turbid, the current is murky.

Thus we know that those who wish to be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss must surely practice the sixteen sublime contemplations; if one aspires to behold the World-Honored Amitābha, one must cultivate these practices.

There are three kinds of pure karma. Yet, transformation proceeds gradually through events, and the teaching arises by relying on conditions. Thus, when King Ajātaśatru committed the crime of parricide, Vaidehī made her plea with grief;
the Great Sage bestowed his compassion and, seizing this opportunity, expounded the Dharma. He radiated the luster of his jade-like marks and manifested auspicious signs from his precious terraces.
Although he extensively revealed the various realms, he pointed toward the Pure Land as the ultimate refuge, so that those in the degenerate age with karmic affinity might follow this path.

In wondrous contemplation, the setting sun hangs like a drum, serving as a signpost for the direction of one’s thoughts; the great waters freeze into ice, truly manifesting the ground of lapis lazuli.
The wind sighs through jeweled leaves, flourishing in harmony with celestial music; the waves ripple upon golden channels, resonating in unison with the sūtras.
Beholding the uṣṇīṣa, one gazes upon the attendant; recollecting the ūrṇā-kośa, one beholds the Tathāgata. And when his eyes close...
Having reached the end [of his life], he ascended the precious terrace and leaped high; as the seal of his marks dissolved, he sat upon a golden lotus and was born through transformation.

Following the three ranks of practitioners, he traversed across [the realms] and galloped eternally beyond the five sufferings. This may truly be called the subtle practice and wondrous contemplation, the essential artifice of the Ultimate Way.
This sutra takes mental visualization as its primary principle and the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) as its essence. Thus it is said: "The Buddha taught the Contemplation of the Infinite Life..."

"Buddha" (Fo): The Buddha is the supreme object of contemplation. By mentioning his primary retribution-body (*vipākaphala*), his attendant fruits are included; by describing the Master of Transformation, his retinue is encompassed.

Although there are sixteen objects of contemplation, the term "Buddha" alone suffices to cover them all. Therefore, it is said: "The Buddha spoke the Sūtra on the Contemplation of Amitāyus Buddha. "Sūtra" (Jing):
This is glossed as "Dharma" and "Eternal," because it was uttered from the golden mouth of the Sage.
Preface to the *Sūtra on the Visualization of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life* by Chan Master Cijue:
The ocean of perfect and universal knowledge arises from the mind’s thoughts; the worlds of all Buddhas are pure lands that follow the mind.

Thus, the Most Holy Amitābha is not separated from the lowliest ordinary person, and although the Land of Ultimate Bliss is distant, how could it be apart from one’s own heart-mind? Therefore, by reciting the Buddha’s name...
One immediately attains the vision of the Buddha; seeking rebirth, one is ultimately able to attain it. As for the *Contemplation Sutra on the Buddha of Immeasurable Life*:

by means of the mind of the Dharma-realm, one illuminates the sphere of true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). The three types of pure karma constitute the direct cause of the Dharma-practice, while the sixteen sublime contemplations serve as the skillful means of quiescent illumination.
Thus, the Dharma-body and the transformation-body accord with capacity, and the environment and the primary retribution are viewed as a single whole. This is...
Because Vaidehī attained great enlightenment and was granted the prophecy of rebirth, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, personally commanded its upholding and extensively expounded these matters.
Although the sutra has been transmitted to this land, it has rarely circulated; were it not for those of perfect capacity, who would present this gift of Dharma?
The Bhikṣu Qiong’an of Changshan and others, pitying that sentient beings in their daily lives do not emerge from the toils of saṃsāra, lamented that the wondrous realm—
It is boundless. I pray that you will act as our guide; let us join in heart to carve these woodblocks so that it may be widely upheld.
This is neither the peerage of Śrāvakas nor the old community of Master Huiyuan. I have briefly composed this preface to universally inform those who have not yet heard it.

The Amitāyus Buddha praises the Great Wisdom Vinaya Master for his eighty-four thousand wondrous marks; is this not the Maitreya of one’s own fundamental nature? Though ten million billion lands lie in distant regions, they are truly the Pure Land of one’s own mind.
Although the pure and the defiled are separated, how could they transcend one’s own mind? Although sentient beings and Buddhas appear distinct, [they are ultimately one].

It would be better to deviate from one's own nature; for the substance of the mind is vast and empty, unimpeded by coming and going. Since its nature is fundamentally all-encompassing, what hindrance could there be to grasping or rejecting?
Thus, with a single thought, one ascends to the Jewel Realm and returns to the ancestral home of the Earth-born.

With a snap of the fingers, one gazes up upon the Compassionate Countenance, truly reuniting as father and son in primordial truth. For how many lifetimes have we been ungrateful for this virtue, needlessly enduring the depths of samsara? Today—

Those who surrender their hearts will surely receive deliverance. With the three minds fully awakened, one's single resolve hastens toward the West. One shall rely upon and follow [the Buddha] until the end of time, praising Him throughout dust-motes and lands.
The *Miaozongchao* on the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Life*:

The Venerable of Siming, Liangjie, maintained that the perfect understanding (*yuanjie*) is entirely distinct from the Lesser Vehicle (*xiǎochéng*). In the Lesser Vehicle, the mind alone exists while the Buddha exists externally;

therefore, the essence of the mind and the Buddha are different. The practitioner of the Mahāyāna knows that their own single mind possesses the nature of all Buddhas, and thus relies upon objects to cultivate contemplation.

The marks of the Buddha are thus manifested. Now, observing that the environment and the beings of Amitābha serve as conditions to permeate the nature of the mind, the environment and beings of Sukhāvatī inherent within the nature of the mind arise through this permeation.
Since they arise from what is inherent in the mind, how could they be separate from the nature of the mind? The entire mind is the Buddha.
All Buddhas are the mind. Throughout the day one contemplates the mind; throughout the day one contemplates the Buddha.
Furthermore, one should realize that the inconceivable essence of the perfectly interfused Dharma-realm constitutes my single thought-moment.

Moreover, this entire essence manifests as sentient beings and as Buddhas, as the support and as the supported, as the sense organs and as their objects. From the single mind to a single speck of dust, it extends to every thing.
Even a single atom does not fail to be the entire dharma-realm manifesting as such.

Since every single phenomenon is the entire dharma-realm manifesting as itself, to cite any one of them is to grasp the entire, perfectly interfused dharma-realm. Since it is the entire dharma-realm, what single thing could there be that does not possess all phenomena?
Furthermore, the fruit—the body of the Buddha’s perfect luminosity—is the inherent nature and virtue possessed by ordinary beings from the very beginning.

Therefore, among all the practices taught in the various teachings, there are none that do not aim to reveal this awakened essence. Thus, this gate of contemplation relies upon the environment and the inhabitants of that Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang).

Employing subtle and profound contemplation, focus exclusively on Amitābha to manifest the essence of the True Buddha. Although one relies upon that external realm, one must know that the environment and its inhabitants (the *shō* and *jō*) coexist within a single mind.
The nature of the mind is all-pervasive; there is no phenomenon that it does not create, and no phenomenon that it does not possess.

If even a single phenomenon were to arise outside of the mind, it could not be called Mahāyāna contemplation. The practitioner should understand this and, based upon the nature of the mind, perform the contemplation.

That [sun] is the environment and the sentient beings; thus the environment and sentient beings may be made manifest. Relying upon that environment and sentient beings, one contemplates the nature of the mind. The nature of the mind is easily brought forth.
The subtle understanding of a person of perfect capacity knows that the mind capable of conceptualization is fundamentally endowed with all phenomena of the environment and sentient beings.

Now, by means of the mind that is already endowed [with these], one takes as an object the sun that is identical to the mind, causing the sun of the original nature to appear before one. This is the application of the Dharma.

The mind of the realm (dhātu-citta) takes the objects of the dharma-realm as its condition and gives rise to the sun of the dharma-realm. Since both are entirely the dharma-realm, how could they not be precisely emptiness, the provisional, and the middle?

Because the faculties and their objects are empty and quiescent, the mind and the sun are unimpeded; because they are provisionally established through dependent origination, the accumulated thoughts arise as the sun.
Because their minds are daily the entire Dharma-realm, they manifest within that very place. These three contemplations are identical within a single mind;
they are neither one nor three, yet they are both three and one—an inconceivable mystery.
The mind-treasury possesses all dharmas; how could it have any limits? Lacking the conditions for sublime contemplation, they remain hidden and do not manifest.
Now, relying on the Buddha’s words, one contemplates them in accordance with their nature. The radiance of the jewel-ground and its various wondrous signs appear in accordance with the mind.

If one wishes to contemplate the Buddha-body, one must know the essence of contemplation. This essence is original enlightenment (*prakṛti-āśraya-jñāna*); it arises to constitute the capacity for contemplation, and it is upon this essence that the fundamental tenet is established—this is what is meant.

One must know that original enlightenment is precisely the Dharma-realm body (*dharmadhātu-kāya*) of all Buddhas, because all Tathāgatas have no separate object of realization, as they fully realize the inherent nature of sentient beings. If initial enlightenment (*ādi-bodhi*) exerts its efficacy, then original enlightenment...
To manifest this, it is said that the Dharma-body arises from the mind and thoughts.

One should know that the contemplation practiced here does not merely involve observing the Buddha of one's own fundamental nature within the aggregates; rather, it relies upon another Buddha to reveal that fundamental nature.

Therefore, the *nirmāṇakāya* (response-body) Buddha manifests; one knows that the fundamental nature is luminous. This is established by relying on external meanings and founded upon the contemplation of "mind-only. It is further said:
One should know that the true mark (*dharmatā*) is in its entirety a luminous illumination, which is termed the "true mind" and also called "original enlightenment" (*mūla-avabodha*).

Because the essence of enlightenment is all-pervasive, all phenomena are real. If one points to its essential core, it is not separate from the present moment of discriminative thought; thought itself is...

Inherent enlightenment (*prakṛti-āśraya-jñāna*): "enlightenment" is the very substance of the sūtra; there is no separate substance of the sūtra that serves as its referent. By means of this awakened mind, one contemplates the environment and its inhabitants;
subject and object are immediately severed, and all dualistic dependencies are forgotten. The principle of sublime contemplation is established from this point onward.
Zhizhi said: "The image sixteen or eight feet tall is provided to accord with those of inferior capacity, enabling them to perceive the great through the small.
All thoughts of coarseness or subtlety arise from cultivation based on nature; all distinct forms of smallness or greatness are manifestations of traces descending from the source.
Since the nature that can observe is originally without differentiation, how could the object observed ever be measured? This discourse of the Perfect and Sudden is a single sound that reaches all."

It reveals the stages of practice without being gradual; it accords with the capacities of beings without being partial. It simultaneously opens the gates of contemplation and fully manifests the true reality (*dharmatā*).
Is not the source of the Semblance Dharma teachings found herein?
The Eulogy on the Divine Abode of An-yang by Chan Master Mizhuo:
The precious realm of Amitābha bears the auspicious name "An-yang" (Peaceful Nurturing). Situated within the land of retribution, it is supremely blissful; among the ten directions, it is most pure.

Through the twenty-eight gates of contemplation, one enters the profound stillness by cultivating the concentrated mind; through the forty great vows, one brings forth the distracted mind to achieve birth by transformation.

Thus, one upholds [the teachings] throughout one’s entire life and takes refuge for a single lifetime. Then, the immortal ascends upon clouds to hear the Dharma, and beings in the void sing hymns in praise.
Upon the purple-golden terrace, one ascends in person, proving that the original vow was not in vain; within the white jade tuft of light, the spirit...

Transformed, they become single-minded and rejoice within themselves. Consider the praise of the broad and long tongue: it is proclaimed simultaneously across ten lands. It merely points to the mind so that all may be in accord;
it is not a hollow transmission based on mere whim. The axis of the earth turns, celestial flowers scatter before them, and in a single thought-moment, the blossoms open.
Upon beholding the Buddha, all attained the sublime fruits; illuminated by a thousandfold radiance, they realized the Dharma and joined the ranks of the former sages.

Examining the past and inferring the present, those reborn there were not few. When their karmic destiny arrived, celestial music filled the sky; when the time came, extraordinary fragrances pervaded the chamber.

Within the single realm of ultimate truth, although the manifestation of signs relies upon the Buddha’s majestic power, the observation of these scenes within the pool of seven treasures arises entirely from the mind.
Thus we know that the Sage’s intent is unfathomable and his responsive resonance is enduring. He transforms the mundane into the sacred in an instant;
he clarifies delusion into awakening in a flash. To unearth the immortal scriptures is truly the art of longevity; to point toward the pure lands is the ultimate destination.

They dwell forever in the land of the deathless. Furthermore, there are world-transcending worthies and Great Beings dwelling amidst the dust of the mundane world. Some practice their vows by burning their bodies or lighting their arms;

others establish their conduct by hanging their stomachs or holding their hearts. They do not follow when celestial music comes to welcome them, nor do they rejoice when heavenly youths request their lives.
Whether atop the peaks of blazing fires or within realms of radiant light, they never again hear the name of the evil destinies. Forever...
Casting aside the baseness of the womb-hell, one’s eyes open and one’s tongue is secured as proof is established; like the ox that butts and the bird that pecks, [the cycle] suddenly ceases.

While dwelling within the Iron City, one must refuse the King’s decree and follow one’s crimson heart; while seated upon the Lotus Throne, one relies on the Buddha’s grace and finds it difficult to abandon the ultimate truth.
Should one ever slander the Triple Gem or violate the precepts, then at the moment the winds and knives force the body apart, one shall face the retribution of karma.
When the mirror reflects one’s form, if one suddenly encounters a true teacher, the inconceivable manifests:

the forest of swords transforms into seven rows of jeweled trees, and the chariots of fire change into lotus ponds of eight virtues. The hells dissolve away, and in profound stillness, all fear completely ceases.

As celestial flowers flew about to lead him forward, a transformation Buddha suddenly appeared to welcome him. His wisdom-eye became clear and his mind enlightened; the incense burner fell from his hand.

In accordance with the prophecy, the lotus flower did not wither; having received the prediction of enlightenment, the Jewel Forest would not remain for long. How marvelous! The power of the Buddha is inconceivable, such as has never existed before in the past or present.
In the *Guide to the Secret Treasury*, the Great Master Ouyi Shouchang said:
"The mind that recites the Buddha's name is itself the Buddha. This is because the present moment of thought is devoid of intrinsic nature and arises through conditions.

That which arises through conditions is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). Precisely because it arises through conditions while lacking intrinsic nature, mindfulness is such that the entire body is name;

mindfulness is such that the entire body is benefit. Even to the point that what is done by day and what is dreamed at night all converge toward the single-pointed concentration of one thought-moment, and from this, the rising and falling within the ten realms emerge.
It is precisely because that which arises through conditions lacks intrinsic nature that [the mind] blazes forth.
However, when creating and accumulating good or evil, if one suddenly lets go, then all phenomena become utterly unobtainable.

Yet, if one sits fixedly within this state of unobtainability, one falls into a deep pit of non-action (*asaṃskṛta*), whereby one cannot realize the unimpeded essence of the *dharmadhātu* nor give rise to its unimpeded function.
Therefore, one must practice mindfulness of the Buddha and seek rebirth in the Pure Land.
This is indeed the inconceivable, perfect, and sudden Dharma-gate of the Mahāyāna. Now, what else could the practice of nianfo (reciting the Buddha's name) be?

It is simply to use this single thought—which is devoid of intrinsic nature because it arises through conditions—to recite the name of that Buddha who is likewise devoid of intrinsic nature and arises through conditions.
Since the names of the Buddhas are devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) and arise dependently, that which arises dependently likewise lacks intrinsic nature.

Therefore, when one recites a single name, one name of a Buddha manifests; when one recites ten, a hundred, a thousand, or ten million names, ten, a hundred, a thousand, or ten million names of Buddhas manifest.
Yet, when not being recited, they are utterly still. Since the nature of recitation is dependently arisen and devoid of intrinsic nature, then...
The absence of intrinsic nature does not obstruct dependent origination. If one does not recite the Buddha’s name, I fear that various miscellaneous thoughts will again arise;
even if such thoughts do not arise, I fear one might fall into the conceptual trap of "non-arising. Therefore, one must certainly give rise to the thought of the Buddha by means of the Buddha-name.
To cause my every thought-moment not to be separated from the Buddha’s name means that there is no Buddha outside the mind, and no mind outside the Buddha.
This mind creates the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha. It may be said that one uses the Buddha to realize the mind, or that one uses the mind to realize the Buddha;
it may also be said that one uses the Buddha to realize the Buddha, or uses the mind to realize the mind. This is most direct, simple, and reliable.
This is the perfectly complete and sudden definitive meaning, which is inconceivable and cannot be measured by comparison with any other dharma-gates.
If you can attain such faith and simply proceed directly from this point, then all Buddhas will extend their broad and long tongues to bear witness to it.
If a person single-mindedly contemplates Amitābha Buddha, this is called the unsurpassed, profound, and wondrous dhyāna.

When one perceives the Buddha through visualization with utmost sincerity, this is precisely the Dharma of non-arising and non-extinction. These are the sincere words of the Golden Mouth; how could they not be believed?
To begin with: the wondrous luminosity of original enlightenment, the dharma-realm of true thusness, is a realm of wisdom and principle where there is no distinction between subject and object;

the environment and its inhabitants are beyond the measures of self and other. It is solely due to delusive ignorance that pervasive conceptualization arises at random; turning one's back on the nature of enlightenment, the nine realms are arrayed in confusion.

When the true realm is obscured, the three lands appear as illusions, causing our World-Honored One laborious toil. Out of compassion, he establishes the teachings according to the faculties and natures of sentient beings, revealing immeasurable Dharma gates.
Sometimes he speaks with explicit clarity; sometimes he speaks with concealed subtlety. For those of partial capacity, he employs indirect means to gradually lead them into the Way;
for those of perfect seed, he directly bestows the teaching to cause immediate enlightenment. Or, from within a single Dharma, he provides detailed explanations.
Whether through immeasurable means or by other skillful expedients (*upāya*), they skillfully assist in revealing the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

Although the nets of teaching are ten thousandfold and diverse, none fail to awaken the long-drawn dream of the nine realms, causing beings to return to the original enlightenment, realize that the three lands are illusory cataracts, and enter into dark resonance with the *sambhogakāya* light (*jigguang*).
Indeed, this is the most ultimate among all ultimate meanings, the most perfectly sudden among all perfect and sudden teachings, and the foremost among all expedient means.
There is no single skillful means (*upāya*) equal to that of the Pure Land. Why is this so? It is because as one's mind becomes pure, so does the Buddha-land become pure.

When afflictions of view and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) are purified, one transcends the Land of Common Dwelling; when afflictions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are purified, one transcends the Land of Skillful Means;

and when ignorance (*avidyā*) is purified, one transcends the Land of Real Reward. Therefore it is said: "Only the Buddha alone dwells in the Pure Land. How could there be any meaning here that is not understood? When sentient beings bring the Buddha to mind with their hearts...
This mind creates the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha. Because one enters the ocean of Buddhas instantaneously in a single thought-moment, it is said:

"Whoever utters 'Namo Buddha' even once has already attained the path of Buddhahood. If a person single-mindedly contemplates Amitābha Buddha, this is called the unsurpassed, profound, and wondrous dhyāna.
Is this not most perfect and sudden? The power of the fruition-virtue and vows is inconceivable; the power of faith in the causal mind is likewise [inconceivable].

Inconceivable! Through the mutual resonance of cause and response, the scriptural text is completed and the seal is broken. By means of an ordinary person, one ascends to the stage of non-retrogression; without severing delusions, one attains transverse transcendence.
Furthermore, the three faculties are universally encompassed, and the four lands are horizontally pervaded. The lightening of the five turbidities occurs within the Land of Common Residence;

the skillful purification through the realization of emptiness occurs within the Land of Expedient Means; and the pure purity of the three contemplations occurs within the Land of Real Reward. This is ultimate awakening.

"Purely abiding in the Land of Quiescent Light, there is not even that which is equal; how much less could there be anything that surpasses it? This is called inconceivable merit, a teaching difficult for the world to believe.
To summarize its essential points, one must possess the three: faith, aspiration, and practice. As for faith, it is faith in phenomena and faith in principle;
faith in oneself and faith in others; faith in the cause and faith in the fruit. One must realize that outside of the mind there is no land, and outside of the land there is no mind."
Outside of nature there is no Buddha; outside of the Buddha there is no nature. The cause necessarily encompasses the fruit, and the fruit necessarily penetrates to the cause.
In terms of aspiration, one should dedicate every thought-moment and direct every mind toward [the goal]. In terms of practice, the immeasurable Dharma-gates all converge into a single consistency.
Among these, the primary practice for the Pure Land is, above all, the recitation of the Buddha's name.
The single thought-moment of our present mind is originally of the same substance as Amitābha Buddha;
yet, that few are able to directly realize this homecoming is due to nothing other than their lack of the three—faith, practice, and vow. I have often said that faith is like a general.
Aspiration should be like a plan; practice should be like an army. With both generals and strategy, even the old and weak can achieve victory;

yet if there is no general or strategy, even the brave and strong will be routed. Therefore, faith should be single-minded, aspiration should be examined with care, and practice should not fail to encompass all.
Because it is single-minded and careful, it is perfect, sudden, direct, and reaches the highest state. Because it encompasses all, it is universally available to those of the three capacities.
It reaches even to the broad masses. This is why the Samādhi of Recollecting the Buddha is so exceptionally superior as a "horizontal transcendence.
Lately, among those of religious and scholarly standing, some regard recollecting the Buddha as too easy, considering it intended only for those of middling or inferior capacity;

others regard it as too difficult, believing that fasting and precepts must be fully observed. Now, if it is too easy, it lacks loftiness; if it is too difficult, it lacks universality. How could this be the Treasure...?
This is what is meant by the King of Samādhis.

The universal teaching of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*— that all things are like illusions and dreams— is spoken in order to shatter the dual attachments to self and dharmas held by ordinary beings, non-Buddhists, and those of the two vehicles.
Now, although the dream-objects are empty, the dreaming mind is itself the awakened mind. Although illusory phenomena are false, the source of the illusion is not entirely void.
Although bubbles lack substance, they are not without water; although shadows lack substance, they are not without a physical basis.
Thus we know that although the cycle of birth and death among the six realms of existence is like an illusion or a dream, the Buddha-nature is never severed or extinguished. It is merely...

It is simply that you do not realize it. A Bodhisattva clearly understands that the nature of the mind in this very moment extends through all past and present, fundamentally being neither born nor extinguished.
It is equal to the Buddhas above and equal to sentient beings below; though one might wish not to seek upward toward the Buddhas or transform those below, it is impossible to avoid doing so.

Nevertheless, although one has resolved upon the Great Bodhicitta, because the habitual tendencies of beginningless, false ignorance are heavy and the power of contemplation is slight, there is cause for apprehension.
It is easy to regress. One must take this perfect understanding and single-mindedly recite the name of Amitābha Buddha, seeking rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
For since the nature of our present single thought is fundamentally vertical and exhaustive, and horizontal and pervasive, it inherently contains boundless oceans of lands.
Within these boundless oceans of lands within my own mind-nature, there truly exists the Land of Ultimate Bliss beyond ten quadrillion worlds.

In the Land of Bliss, there truly exists the present Buddha Amitābha. Having first realized the nature of the mind, he compassionately draws in all those wandering in delusion. Now, by means of this power of bodhicitta, I invoke his name;

thus, I am one with Amitābha Buddha, like space merging with space and water merging with water. Therefore, with each single invocation of the name, that single sound is the non-distraction of the single mind.

To recite the name ten times is to maintain single-mindedness without distraction for those ten recitations; even to recite the name for seven days is to maintain single-mindedness without distraction for those seven days.
This is because at the very moment of the correct recitation, there is no second thought and nothing further that can cause distraction.
On the Discourse Concerning Nianfo as Chan Meditation:
Someone asked Master Ouyi about the practice of Chan meditation and doctrinal contemplation compared to the Dharma-gate of Nianfo (Buddha-recitation). He replied:

"To speak of them as being the same or different is mere frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*). To say they are both the same and different, or neither the same nor different, is likewise frivolous proliferation."

Because there are no phenomena that are not free from the four extremes through these three gateways of Dharma, if one knows that all phenomena are none other than the self-nature of mind, they can still be expressed and revealed by means of the four extremes.
What is this? In the Sanskrit language it is *dhyāna*; here [in Chinese] it is called *ching-lü* (meditative concentration).

Quiescence (*śamatha*) is concentration (*samādhi*); deliberation (*vipaśyanā*) is wisdom (*prajñā*). Quiescence is cessation (*śamatha*); deliberation is contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). Quiescence is stillness (*śānti*); deliberation is illumination (*prabhāsvara*).

Therefore, concentration and wisdom, cessation and contemplation, and stillness and illumination are all one essence with different names. Some say that "stillness and illumination" refers to the nature (*prakṛti*), while the other two refer to cultivation (*bhāvanā*);
"cessation and contemplation" refers to the cause (*hetu*), while "concentration and wisdom" refers to the fruit (*phala*). This is merely a superficial distinction.
I shall simply say this: although the nature of the mind in each present thought of ours may be clouded by delusion and inverted confusion, its luminous awareness can never be extinguished;
and although it flows through the cycle of existence in a state of turmoil, its fundamental substance has never wavered. Is this not the true source of quiescent illumination?
The lifeblood of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* is found in concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). To investigate this present momentary mind-nature is called "investigating Chan" (*chán*).

To penetrate this present momentary mind-nature is called "stopping and observing" (*zhíguān*). To contemplate and maintain awareness of this present momentary mind-nature is called "reciting the Buddha's name" (*niànfó*).
For "mindfulness" (*niàn*) is the wisdom of initial awakening (*shíjué*), and "Buddha" (*fó*) is original awakening (*běnjué*).

This is the principle. Within this Dharma gate of Buddha-recollection, there are differences depending on whether one recollects the Buddha within oneself, the Buddha outside oneself, or both the self and other Buddhas.
If one recollects only the Buddha within oneself, it is entirely identical to Chan meditation and *śamatha-vipaśyanā*.

If one recollects only the Buddha outside oneself, it is both different from and the same as Chan meditation and *śamatha-vipaśyanā*. If one recollects both the self and other Buddhas, it is neither different from nor the same as Chan meditation and *śamatha-vipaśyanā*.

It is the same. Now, as for "mindfulness of one's own Buddha," this is the practice of the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*), namely: the contemplation of the body, the contemplation of feelings, the contemplation of the mind, and the contemplation of phenomena (*dharmas*).

If any dharma-gate were not subsumed within these four foundations of mindfulness, it would be a teaching of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). Therefore, we know that it is identical to meditative contemplation (*dhyāna-vipaśyanā*).

As for "mindfulness of another Buddha," this may involve mindfulness of the physical marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), or mindfulness of the dharma-gates, or mindfulness of the true reality (*bhūta-lakṣaṇa*).
If one is unable to perform these three types of recollection, then one should simply hold the name.

Although recollecting the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) may at first glance appear different from meditative contemplation (*dhyāna*), if one necessarily ceases all distracting conditions and focuses exclusively on that Buddha, it remains identical to *samādhi*.

Recollection of the Dharma-gate can be understood by analogy with this. Even when recollecting the true reality (*bhūta-lakṣaṇa*), although it relies upon the Buddha as the fruit of others, [it is still meditation].

They are different; yet, in the end, there are never two kinds of true reality (*dharmatā*). Ultimately, they are the same. If one holds the name of the Buddha, at first glance this may differ from meditative contemplation (*dhyāna-vipaśyanā*);
however, regardless of whether one understands it or not, the name being held is, in its very essence, nothing other than the single realm of the three truths.
The mind that holds it is, in its very essence, nothing other than the single mind of the three contemplations. Therefore, it is said: "A bright pearl is cast into..."
In turbid water, the turbidity cannot fail to clear; when the name of the Buddha is cast into a distracted mind, the distraction cannot fail to become unified.
Thus, when the mind has no other objects, this is stillness and cessation (*śamatha*); when the names are distinct and clear, this is reflection and contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).

These are ultimately the same. Now, as for those who recollect both themselves and others as Buddhas, they thoroughly understand that the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings are three [aspects of one reality].

There is no difference. It is by relying upon other Buddhas that one’s original nature is revealed; because one awakens to this original nature, it is not different from meditative contemplation (*dhyāna*).
Because it relies upon other Buddhas, it is not the same as meditative contemplation. This is called the supreme and extraordinary skillful means, the unsurpassed Dharma-gate.
The *Mañjuśrī-prajñā-sūtra*, the *Pratyutpanna-samādhi-sūtra*, the *Amitāyurdhyāna-sūtra*, and others all elucidate this.
This is the definitive meaning of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching, which the *Miaozongchao* (The Subtle Commentary on the Title) explains in detail.
All practitioners who have set their minds upon the Pure Land must thoroughly investigate this and strive to put it into practice.
The Origin of Pure Practice at Lingfeng Temple:

I have observed that the excellence of the Pure Land does not reside primarily in the lands of *sukhāvatī* (the land of tranquil light), *vipākaphala* (recompense), or *upāya* (expedient means); rather, it lies in the land of shared residence (*sahabhūmi*).

For while birth in the former three lands requires the severance of delusions, the land of shared residence is entered directly through the mutual guidance of faith and aspiration, wherein the path of resonance and response unfolds.
Through this [practice], the habits of the five turbidities are gradually lightened and the sufferings of the three realms are thereby liberated.

Furthermore, within this very Land of Ultimate Bliss in the West, one vertically penetrates through the stages of Expedient Means, True Reward, and the Quiescent Light. Thus, even those of the lowest capacity may cross its threshold, while those of the highest wisdom can never transcend its bounds.
It universally sustains the three faculties and fully provides for the four purposes (*catus-saṃgraha-vastu*). While the True Dharma remains in the world, all the Patriarchs have already...
To propagate [the Dharma] during this degenerate age when people are lost at the ford: how could the Four Reliances fail to offer singular praise?

Thus, those who claim to "ride the carriage" of direct pointing treat the Western Land as a mere placeholder; those who study the Mahayana through words alone regard Pure Land as a place for retirement.

They do not contemplate that, without relying on expedient means, one may spontaneously attain the opening of the mind. How could there be such a circuitous path? With exquisite flowers filling their satchels, they offer them everywhere to hundreds of millions.
How can there truly be such a thing as the Small Vehicle? Moreover, since you have already awakened to the direct pointing, this is called "seeing one's nature and becoming a Buddha.
For what reason do you exclude Amitābha from within your own nature? Since you ride upon great vows, you must necessarily adorn and purify a buddha-land;

for what reason do you single out the Land of Ultimate Bliss from among the ocean of lands? Indeed, in the provisional teachings of the Śrāvakas, the names of Buddhas in other directions are not heard. (4)

The efficacy of his spiritual power extends only within the three-thousandfold world system. As for those ten thousand distant regions, who—other than the Supreme Lotus Great Being, the Heroic Man—is capable of drawing near to and serve the Exalted and Wondrous Sugata?
Having just been nurtured upon the lotus throne, he immediately attained the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*).

Compared to those who resolve their minds to investigate the truth and expect to achieve it in three lifetimes, he has already awakened to the essence of the mind; yet he still speaks of "never retreating throughout successive births."
That the stage of Buddhahood can be anticipated—whether it be difficult or easy, slow or swift—is clearly discernible.

how could it be said that the Buddha is not produced by mind? In the year Jisi (1549), I met the elder Zheng Qianli.

[This] word would cause people to burst into laughter. The *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra-gāthā* says: "If a person merely recollects Amitābha, this is called the unsurpassed, profound, and wondrous dhyāna.

A Memorial for the Encouragement of Nianfo by the Śrāmaṇera Rencao:

The Tathāgata Amitābha gathers and transforms beings throughout the ten directions through his forty-eight vows; the Great Being Avalokiteśvara (Śrī-vidyut-dhara) wanders through this world by means of the samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha.
One should know that sentient beings of the final age who abandon the single gate of the Pure Land to seek liberation elsewhere [will find none].
Birth and death cannot be found; the Buddha-dharma is not something vast. It is difficult for people to encounter it over the long course of time.

A moment of fierce diligence is not as good as a lifelong lack of weariness. I have long cultivated this Samādhi of Buddha-Recollection. Every day, I begin with one hundred thousand recitations and proceed down to one hundred, or even just ten;
at the very least, I recite a single time per day. Regardless of whether the number is many or few, my rule is simply that there be no interruption throughout my entire life.
I shall take this practice—like eating when hungry and drinking when thirsty—as the deed of title for the precious land and the sublime pond. Even so, I am still able to...

suddenly cuts off views and thoughts and thereby transcends the Land of Expedient Means.

Even if one has not yet severed the delusions, the five turbidities gradually clear, the Buddha’s light gradually reveals itself, and one ascends to the Land of Shared Residence, forever liberated from saṃsāra—there can be no doubt of this. May all beings universally aspire to this!
