The Essential Points of Buddha-Recitation:
Chan Master Chewu states that the present single thought of our own—the mind capable of reciting—is entirely true yet fully delusory; entirely delusory yet precisely true.

Throughout the day we follow conditions, yet throughout the day we remain unchanging. The single phrase of the Buddha who is recited is a name established based on complete virtue; apart from this virtue, there is no name.

One invokes virtue by means of its name; outside the name, there is no virtue. One can contemplate that outside the mind, there is no separate Buddha who is the object of contemplation, and outside the Buddha who is contemplated, there is no separate mind that contemplates.
Subject and object are non-dual, yet the sentient being and the Buddha appear distinct. Fundamentally, they are free from the four extremes.
Fundamentally transcending all negations, fundamentally pervading all things, and fundamentally containing all things, it is absolute, perfectly interfused, and inconceivable.
Practitioners of the Lotus School should enter through faith from this very point. It is further said: "One utterance of the Buddha’s name is one utterance of the mind;
it is clear and distinct right here—what need is there to seek it elsewhere? There is no need to repeatedly brandish the whip; the white ox has already drawn forth the ancient gold."
It is further said: "The nine grades of precious lotuses are beneath one's heels; if one does not recite the name of Amitābha, one betrays oneself.

As for the Master Zhiyi’s [practice of] *zhiguan* (calming and contemplation) and his engagement in worldly affairs (*yuanwu*), such interference with meditation has been a long-standing problem. How can a forest-dwelling bhikṣu, who has left the clamor for tranquility, engage in construction?"
Worldly affairs ruin the practice of the araṇya; they are not appropriate for one [in such a state]. There are four kinds of worldly affairs: first, livelihood; second, social obligations;
third, technical skills; and fourth, learning. Regarding the worldly affair of livelihood: it involves managing the means of subsistence, which becomes entangled and complicated at every turn.

To gain one thing is to lose another; this leads to the loss of the Way and the disordering of the mind. As for the two types of human affairs—the observances of celebration and mourning, and the formalities of bowing and rising, lowering and raising oneself during visits—these involve going here and coming there, with the flow of traffic never ceasing.
How much more so when many people are entangled in a web of social ties, bustling about in pursuit of them?

Now, you have left your kin and parted from your teacher, originally seeking the essential Way, yet you have instead formed connections across three provinces and reinforced those in five commanderies. What do you intend to achieve by this? It is a complete reversal.
To wear a skirt with a corded collar, or to seek ice by drilling for fire, is not what is appropriate. As for the three skills—medical arts, divination, and the crafting of clay, wood, or paint;
chess, calligraphy, and incantations—and so forth: even if one possesses beautiful hide-patterns, fine horns, or refined oils and broths, one will ultimately destroy oneself.
How much more so when practicing the supramundane Way! It is like a forest attracting birds or a putrid odor drawing flies; how could this not be so?

To be broken, crushed, defiled, and humiliated—this refers to the four types of scholars who engage in the reading and recitation of sutras and treatises, as well as debates on points of victory and defeat.
To retain and memorize these texts exhausts the mind and weary the will; the back-and-forth of such discourse clouds the water and dims the pearl.
How could there be leisure to further cultivate *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*? If one must abandon even this matter, how much more so the three prior tasks? And so forth.
Regarding those who observe the mind in their daily lives: craving is the method by which karma is nourished, just as water moistens a seed.
Because of craving there is sorrow; because of sorrow there is fear. If one can sever craving, it is called bringing rest to the conditions and affairs of life.

Human affairs are karma; karma gives rise to the three realms and causes one to wander through the five destinies. With craving moistening karma, one undergoes birth in every place. If there were no karma, craving [would have nothing to moisten].
There is nothing to moisten. Although all karmas possess power, they do not follow one who does not perform them; because one does not perform them, birth and death are severed.
One who possesses technical skill, yet has not attained the Noble Path, cannot cultivate the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). False and illusory phenomena obstruct *prajñā*. *Prajñā* is like space:
it is free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and devoid of words and letters. If one attains *prajñā*, it is like obtaining a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*). However...

Cultivate with a single mind; why be so hasty? Those who employ supernatural powers as their practice have not yet attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*), yet they cultivate worldly wisdom and eloquence.
All such various discriminations are merely shards, rubble, grass, and wood—they are not true jewels.
If one can remain still, the water will become clear, and one may look down upon the lapis lazuli and calmly retrieve the treasure. Thus, one is able to know the arising of the world.

The characteristics of phenomena are extinguished; what kind of various modes of existence could there be that he does not know? He knows them with the knowledge of all modes and sees them with the Buddha-eye.
One who wishes to practice the Great Way should not train in those minor paths.

He censures the five desires (*pañca-kāma-guṇa*). The five desires refer to forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles. The *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "To restrain the six sense-faculties is like tethering a dog, a deer, a fish, a snake, a monkey, and a bird.
The dog delights in the village; the deer delights in the mountains and marshes; the fish delights in the ponds and pools; the snake delights in its burrow."
Dwelling thus: monkeys delight in deep forests, birds delight in relying upon the void, and the six sense faculties delight in the six objects.
This is not something that can be subdued by the shallow wisdom and weak resolve of ordinary people; only through wisdom, a firm mind, and right mindfulness can they be subdued.

This serves as a general metaphor for the six sense faculties; now I shall apply it specifically. The eye craves forms; forms possess substance and appearance like a village, and the eye is like a dog.
The ear craves sound; sound has no substantial form, being like an empty marsh, while the ear is like a deer. The nose craves fragrance like a fish; the tongue seeks out flavors like a snake;
the body clings to touch like a monkey; the mind dwells upon mental objects like a bird. Now, setting aside the faculty of mind, we clarify the five sense-objects (*pañca-viṣaya*).
These five objects are not themselves desire, yet within them there are flavors that can give rise to the cravings of the practitioner.
Because of the mind of desire, they are called the "five desires" (*pañca-kāma*). It is like a potter who, when invited by a patron, cannot apply himself to his craft;
the five desires are likewise always able to drag a person into the realms of Māra. Even if one possesses the preceding conditions, it is difficult for the mind to remain composed;
therefore, they must be censured. As for sensual form (*rūpa*), this refers to [features such as] red and white, long and short, bright eyes with a fine gaze, a fair neck, and emerald-green eyebrows.

With white teeth and crimson lips, even down to their external environments (*niśraya-vipāka*), there are objects of red, yellow, vermilion, and purple, as well as various precious treasures that agitate and move the human heart.

As explained in the Chan school, the harm of sensory form (*rūpa*) is particularly deep; it causes people to become intoxicated with madness, for this is precisely the root of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).

For instance, although Nanda maintained his precepts out of desire and attained the stage of Arhat, his residual habits (*vāsanā*) were still numerous; how much more so for those who are still bound by all fetters?

This is so! The king is addicted to excess and lacks restraint; disregarding the gravity of the ancestral temple and the altars of the state, he enters the enemy’s realm for the sake of sensual pleasure.
Throughout our own past dynasties, the ruin of states and the destruction of families have mostly arisen from such desire. How magnificent was the House of Zhou! Yet it fell because of this.
"Bao Si destroyed it. This refers to that very event. The Sūtra says: "Sentient beings are greedily covetous of wealth and beauty;
because of this, they fail to attain the Way. The *Guanjing* says: "One is driven by the 'envoy of form' (rūpa-dūta); being so driven, one becomes a slave to affection and cannot attain self-mastery.

If one can recognize the faults and afflictions of form, then one will not be deceived by it. Having thus rebuked [the mind], desire for form immediately ceases, and conditioned thoughts do not arise.

One enters meditative concentration with single-minded focus. Regarding the desire for sound: this refers to seductive and alluring words, lewd sounds and defiling speech, as well as the sounds of stringed and wind instruments, such as those of bracelets, bangles, and bells. Regarding the desire for fragrance:

this refers to dense and pervasive scents, such as the aroma of orchids and musk, fragrant and potent substances, and the bodily odors of men and women. Regarding the desire for taste: this refers to...
These are wine, meat, and delicacies—fatty, oily, sweet, sour, or pungent; ghee, fresh blood, and the like.

As for the objects of desire (*kāmaguṇa*), they consist of cold and warmth, smoothness and softness, lightness and heaviness, strength and suppleness; these include fine garments, superior clothing, the bodies of men and women, and so forth.
These five objects of affliction are like glowing balls of hot gold: to grasp them is to be burned. Their sounds are like drums smeared with poison.

To hear of them is to face certain death. Their fragrance is like the breath of a fierce dragon; to smell it brings illness. Their taste is like boiling honey; to scald the tongue with it causes it to rot.

They are like a blade smeared with honey; to lick it results in injury. To touch them is like lying near a sleeping lion; to draw near, one is bitten. These five desires bring no satiety when obtained;
they cause evil intentions to blaze ever more fiercely, like fire fed with fuel. From lifetime to lifetime, their harm is more severe than [any other].

"O enemy-thieves! For countless kalpas you have constantly plundered me, crushing both my physical form and my mind. Now that I am finally settled in meditative stillness (*dhyāna*), you again trouble and disturb me.
I deeply recognize this transgression; I shall cease this greedy attachment. The details of these phenomena are fully explained in the *Chanmen* (The Gate of Meditation), etc.

A famous monk of former times wrote in verse: 'To distance oneself from them is easy for a man of integrity; to draw near to them is difficult for one's own feelings. Fragrances and flavors cause lofty resolve to decline.'"
Sound and form destroy one’s physical frame and lifespan.

One must abandon the five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*). These five hindrances are: namely, sensual desire, ill-will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt. They are collectively termed "hindrances" because they cover and obscure [the mind].
They are entangling; they darken the mind and spirit, preventing concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) from arising; therefore, they are called "hindrances" (*nīvaraṇa*).
Previously, the five desires were censured because they involve the five sense faculties encountering the five present sensory objects to produce the five consciousnesses.

Now, abandoning the five hindrances refers to these very five consciousnesses turning into the mental ground (*manobhūmi*), where they retrospectively pursue past objects and prospectively speculate about the future. Such phenomena as the five sensory objects constitute a great obstacle within the mind; this is the metaphor.
It is like a potter who, having an ailment in his body, is unable to work; such is the case here as well.

Since the hindrance is profound, one must apply abandonment—just as one cuts down a poisonous tree or apprehends a thief, it must not be retained. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "Free from desires and unwholesome dharmas.
Here, "desires" refers to the five sensual desires, as previously censured; "unwholesome dharmas" refers to the five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*). One should [abandon them].

One must quickly abandon them. What are the characteristics of these five hindrances? When the hindrance of sensual desire arises, one recalls the five objects of desire experienced in the past, dwelling on pure forms that confront the eye;
one remembers lovely sounds as if they were still echoing in the ear; one thinks of pleasing fragrances, which open the gateway to the fetters;
one imagines delicious flavors, with sweet juices flowing into the mouth; and one recalls receiving various tactile sensations, causing the hair on the body to stand on end.

They engage in violent conflict; they crave such coarse and debased five sensual pleasures. Through their thoughts and calculations, their minds become intoxicated and deluded, causing them to lose right mindfulness.
They may secretly employ expedient means in hopes of further obtaining them, or if they have not yet obtained them, they continue to search for them.
Or perhaps one seeks after objects, the mind entering into sensory realms without a moment’s interval of mindfulness; coarse perception thus obstructs dhyāna. How then can dhyāna be attained?

This is called the characteristic of the hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa*). As for the hindrance of ill-will (*vyāpāda-nīvaraṇa*): one repeatedly recalls how a person has harmed oneself, harmed one's kin, or praised one's enemies;

through these nine types of resentment across the three times, enmity and hatred are bound together, the heart becomes feverish, the breath becomes coarse, and anger continues in succession. (The hindrance of sloth-and-torpor follows...)

One plots and waits, desiring to strike and harm another; seeking to endanger the other for one’s own security, one indulges in poisonous anger, taking pleasure in the full expression of one's passions.

Such a fire of hatred burns away all merits; how then could the branches and twigs of meditative concentration (dhyāna) grow? This is the characteristic of the hindrance of ill-will (*vyāpāda-nīvaraṇa*).

As for the hindrance of sloth-and-torpor (*styāna-middha-nīvaraṇa*): the mind and spirit are shrouded in darkness, which is torpor; the six consciousnesses are blocked and obstructed, while the four limbs [of the body] are slumped and relaxed.

This is called sleep. Sleep is a mental factor (*caitasika-dharma*) that increases [delusion]; it is dark, murky, and obstructive. It comes secretly and covers a person, making it difficult to guard against.
The five sense faculties lose their consciousness, becoming like those of a dead person; with only a fragment of breath remaining, this is called "minor death. If one delights in sleep...
Sleep increases excessively. The *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* states: "If a person sleeps much, indolence obstructs their attainment;
that which is not yet attained will not be attained, and that which has already been attained will be lost. If one desires to attain the supreme path, one must eliminate sleep, doubt, and negligence;
by exerting diligence and rousing all mindfulness, one leaves behind evil and accumulates merit. The *Śāstra* further says: "Sleep is a great darkness in which nothing is seen, day after day..."

Deceiving and robbing others of their clarity is like standing amidst the white blades on a battlefield, like dwelling in the same room as a venomous snake, or like being bound and led away to execution—at such times, how could one find peace in sleep?
Sleep obstructs dhyāna, and its fault is most grave; this is called the characteristic of the hindrance of sloth-and-torpor (*styāna-middha-nīvaraṇa*).
As for agitation-and-regret (*auddhatya-kaukṛtya*): if vitarka and vicāra arise excessively, they are subsumed under the preceding hindrance. Now...
Vitarka and vicāra arise and universally take all phenomena as their object. At times they take desire as their object, and at others they imagine anger and delusion;
they blaze forth without ceasing and stand out without abiding. Rising and subsiding alternately, they are manifold and chaotic.

The body wanders aimlessly, and the mouth engages in useless chatter and laughter. This is called *auddhatya* (restlessness). If one is restless yet feels no remorse, it does not constitute a hindrance (*nīvaraṇa*), because...
Because of restlessness, one dwells on thoughts in the mind, lacking caution and moderation. How can one perform such useless actions? This is truly shameful.

When the mind is filled with sorrow and regret, and resentment knots together and缠绕 (entangles) the heart, it becomes the "cover of remorse" (*kaukṛtya-nīvaraṇa*). This shroud covers meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), preventing its development.
If a person repents their past deeds, reproaches their own heart, and gives rise to sorrow and regret, yet enters meditative concentration, [they will succeed].
One should simply recognize one's transgressions and not harbor attachments to them through conceptualization. Liberation is attained not merely by means of remorse;
rather, one should cultivate meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), which is the pure Dharma. How could one allow remorse to entangle the mind and obstruct this great matter?

Therefore it is said: "Once you have repented, do not grieve further. One should not constantly dwell upon thoughts [of past errors]. To do what should not be done, or to fail to do what should be done—this is precisely the meaning [of the teaching].

This is called the characteristic of the hindrance of restlessness and remorse (*auddhatya-kaukṛtya-nīvaraṇa*). As for the hindrance of doubt (*vicikitsā-nīvaraṇa*), this is not the doubt that obstructs the principle of seeing the truths;

rather, it is the doubt that obstructs meditative concentration (*samādhi*). There are three kinds of doubt: first, doubt regarding oneself; second, doubt regarding the teacher; and third, doubt regarding the Dharma.

First, doubt regarding oneself means thinking, "My own person is base and inferior; I certainly am not a vessel for the Path. Thus, one doubts one's own body. Second, doubt regarding the teacher refers to this person...
My body and speech do not accord with my inner aspirations; why must I serve a teacher of profound dhyāna and excellent wisdom?

Might this not lead me astray? Third, regarding doubt concerning the Dharma: "Is the Dharma I have received truly consistent with the Middle Way? These three doubts and hesitations constantly dwell within my breast;

thus, meditative concentration does not arise, and even if it were to arise, it would be lost forever. This is the characteristic of the hindrance of doubt. These are the maladies of the five hindrances.
The characteristics are thus. As for the abandonment of dharmas, the practitioner should examine themselves: "In my mind at present, which affliction is most prevalent?

If one knows the affliction, one should first treat it. If the hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa*) is heavy, one should abandon it by means of the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).
Why? Because previously one regarded the five desires as pure and was bound by attachment; now, observing them as impure, [one sees them as] a bag of pus.
Tears and saliva—there is not a single thing here worth rejoicing in. A sense of revulsion arises, as if one were being pursued by an enemy. What wise person would take pleasure in this?
Therefore, know that this contemplation is the medicine for treating greed; once this veil is removed, the mind immediately attains peace.
If the veil of anger and resentment is great, one should contemplate loving-kindness (*maitrī*) to extinguish the fire of hatred. This fire can burn away the merit of both worlds. O person!
I take no pleasure in seeing them; they are poisonous, harmful, and violent, no different from beasts. As enemies in the cycle of birth and death, our enmity will not cease for kalpas.
A slight resentment in this life becomes a great hatred hereafter. Now, cultivating a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), I shall abandon these evils.

Regarding all people, I shall regard them as my parents and kin, wishing that they all obtain happiness. If they do not obtain happiness, I shall diligently apply my mind to ensure they attain peace and joy. How?
Why harbor resentment toward them? When one contemplates in this way, the mind of anger immediately subsides, and the mind settles to enter meditative absorption (*dhyāna*).

If the hindrance of sleep (*middha-nīvaraṇa*) is excessive, one should apply diligent effort (*vīrya*), exerting both body and mind, and with increased vigilance, contemplate the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).

Discriminate and select between wholesome and unwholesome dharmas; do not allow the hindrance of sleep to enter. Furthermore, you should discern between wholesome and unwholesome states of mind so that joy in the Dharma arises.
Once the mind is clear and pure, the hindrance of sleep will naturally be eliminated. Do not, on account of sleep, [neglect this].

One loses the happiness of both worlds; one’s life is lived in vain and dies in vain, with nothing at all gained. It is like entering a mountain of jewels and returning empty-handed—this is truly a matter for deep lamentation.

One should therefore skillfully restrain the mind and employ clever means of defense. [The methods include] using a staff, a ball, a conch, stretching the legs, rising at the stars, or washing with water.

If the mind remains distracted and scattered, one should apply the practice of counting the breaths (*ānāpānasmṛti*). Why is this? Because this method is extremely effective; when [the mind] comes [to a state of concentration], it does not...

One awakens to this only after a long time. Now, one employs the practice of counting the breaths. If the counting is not accomplished, or if one occasionally forgets, one should immediately realize that [the mind] has already departed;

having awakened, one counts again. When the characteristics of counting are perfected, vitarka and vicāra are subdued. If one does not treat this, one will be shrouded by them for the rest of one's life.
If the three doubts remain in the heart, one should form this thought: "My body is like that of a blind child born into a great wealthy family. It is fully...
One possesses the supreme treasure of the Dharma-body, yet it is obscured by afflictions; the eye of the Path has not yet opened and must be cultivated and purified, never to be abandoned.
Furthermore, what certainty can there be regarding the causal conditions practiced over immeasurable kalpas? How could one allow oneself to doubt them? Time is lost when the opportunity is missed;
a human body is difficult to obtain, and a mind of dread is difficult to arouse. Do not let yourself be ruined by doubt. If you should doubt the teacher...
I am currently without wisdom. Great and holy beings all seek their Dharma and do not take their person as the measure.

The Snowy Mountains [sage] requested verses from a ghost; the Lord of Devas bowed to an animal and took it as his teacher. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "One does not discard gold because of the stench of its bag.

When pride is like a high mountain, rainwater cannot remain upon it; when one is humble like the ocean or rivers, ten thousand streams flow back to gather there. For the sake of the Dharma, I have furthermore...
One should revere them. The *Puchao jing* (Sutra on Universally Transcending) says: "When people meet one another, do not treat each other as equals.
Only one whose wisdom is like that of a Tathāgata can truly level the person. This refers to the meaning of the passage:
"This person enters saṃsāra; this person enters nirvāṇa. One should always give rise to reverence. The Tathāgatas of the three periods of time are one's teachers, including those yet to come.
"O Buddhas, why should I harbor doubts? If I were to doubt the Dharma, it would mean my eye of Dharma has not yet opened and I have not yet distinguished right from wrong;
I would merely be relying on faith. The Buddha-Dharma is like the ocean; only through faith can one enter it. As the *Lotus Sūtra* says:

'The various śrāvakas and others are beyond the scope of their own wisdom; they enter by means of faith. I am as blind and ignorant, yet I do not believe or accept [the teaching]. To whom else could I turn? Long...
Sunk in eternal drowning, they do not know the essential way out. If the mind believes in the Dharma, yet the Dharma defiles the mind, then with hesitation and doubt,
the matter is like an overturned vessel regarding the inconceivable realm.
Regarding the inconceivable realm: as the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states, "The mind is like a skilled painter, creating the various five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
Within all worlds, there is nothing that is not created by the mind. The "various five aggregates" refers to the five aggregates of the ten dharma-realms (*dharmadhātu*).

As for the term "dharma-realm," it has three meanings: the number ten is that which depends; the dharma-realm is that upon which it depends; these two, the dependent and the supported, are combined into a single designation.

Therefore, they are called the "ten dharma-realms" (*daśa-dharmadhātu*). Furthermore, these ten dharmas each have their own respective causes and respective fruits, and are not confused or intermingled;
thus, they are called the ten dharma-realms. Moreover, each of these ten dharmas, in its very essence, is itself the dharma-realm; hence they are called the ten dharma-realms, and so forth.

Regarding the ten dharma-realms, they are collectively designated as aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and realms (*dhātu*); yet in reality, they are not the same. The three miserable paths (*tridurgati*) are characterized by outflows (*sāsrava*).

The "evil" [category] refers to the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases (*skandha-dhātu-āyatana*). The three types of "wholesome" are the contaminated wholesome aggregates, elements, and sense-bases.

Those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) possess uncontaminated aggregates, elements, and sense-bases. Bodhisattvas possess both contaminated and uncontaminated aggregates, elements, and sense-bases.

Buddhas possess aggregates, elements, and sense-bases that are neither contaminated nor uncontaminated. The *Śāstra* states: "That which is supreme among dharmas is nirvāṇa; it is neither contaminated nor uncontaminated."

It is a dharma of outflow (*āsrava*). The *Anantārthasūtra* states: "The Buddha has no great aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), or bases (*āyatana*); he lacks the aforementioned nine aggregates, elements, and bases.

That which is said to exist now refers to the existence of the aggregates, elements, and bases of the eternally abiding nirvāṇa. The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* says: "By the cessation of impermanent form, one obtains eternal form;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so. This is the superimposition of permanence and bliss."

This has the meaning of accumulation. Furthermore, the covering of compassion has the meaning of the aggregates (*skandha*). Because there are ten different types of aggregates and elements (*dhātu*), it is called the "world of the five aggregates" (*pañcaskandhaloka*).

The five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) collectively constitute what is called a "sentient being" (*sattva*). Sentient beings are not uniform: those who grasp the aggregates of the three miserable realms are sentient beings of sinful suffering;

those who grasp the aggregates of humans and devas are sentient beings who experience pleasure; those who grasp the untainted aggregates (*anāsrava-skandha*) are sentient beings who are true sages; those who grasp the aggregates of compassion are sentient beings who are Great Beings (*mahāsattva*);
and those who grasp the eternally abiding aggregates are sentient beings of supreme honor. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Among sentient beings, the unsurpassed is the Buddha."
This is so. How could it be the same as that of ordinary beings? A Great Sūtra states: "At the stage of the *kalala*, the name is different;

up to the stage of old age, the name is different. At the stage of the sprout, the name is different; up to the stage of the fruit, the name is likewise different. This is stated simply in terms of a single lifetime.
There are distinctions among the ten periods of time; how much more so for the sentient beings of the ten realms? How could they not be diverse? Therefore, it is called the "world of sentient beings.
As for the ten kinds of dwellings, which are collectively termed the "world of the physical environment": hell-dwellers rely on red-hot iron; animals rely on earth, water, and space;
asuras rely on the shores and depths of the ocean; humans rely on the earth; and devas rely on palaces.

Regarding their abodes: Bodhisattvas of the Six Perfections dwell on the same stages as humans. Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching, whose afflictions are not yet exhausted, dwell on the same levels as humans and devas;

those who have exhausted their afflictions dwell in the Land of Expedient Means. Bodhisattvas of the Distinct and Complete Teachings, whose afflictions are not yet exhausted, dwell on the same levels as humans, devas, and the Land of Expedient Means;
those who have exhausted their afflictions dwell in the Land of Real Reward. The Tathāgata dwells in the Constant Quiescence.
The Radiant Land Abode (*Prabhāsa-bhūmi*). The *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* states: "The three stages of worthiness and the ten stages of sagehood abide in retributive fruition;

only the Buddha alone dwells in the Pure Land. Since these lands differ from one another, they are termed the "world of lands" (*kṣetra-loka*). These thirty types of worlds are all created by the mind.
Furthermore, there are ten kinds of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), each possessing ten dharmas. These are:

suchness of characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), nature (*svabhāva*), essence (*tattva*), function (*kriyā*), cause (*hetu*), condition (*pratyaya*), fruit (*phala*), retribution (*vipāka*), beginning and end (*pūrvāntāparānta*), and ultimate equality (*samyañc-pariniṣṭhā*). First, a general explanation; second, an explanation according to their respective categories. Regarding the general explanation:

as for "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*), it refers to that which is external and can be distinguished upon observation. The *Śāstra* states: "Because it is easy to know, it is called a characteristic," just like the characteristics of water and fire.

Differences are thus easy to discern. It is like a person’s facial complexion, which manifests all signs of fortune and misfortune; by observing the external features, one immediately knows what lies within.

In the past, when the physiognomists observed the prominent features of Sun Quan and Liu Bei and the hidden features of Cao Cao, they raised their voices and wept aloud. The four seas were divided into three parts, and the common people suffered bitter torment.

If one says there *is* such physiognomy, those who are ignorant do not perceive it; if one says there *is not* such physiognomy, the diviners understand it through and through. This is how it ought to be.
Regarding those who follow the virtuous marks: they believe that the person’s face externally possesses all the marks; the mind is likewise so, possessing all the marks.
Although the marks of ordinary beings are obscured, the marks of Maitreya are manifest. Because the Tathāgata knows this well, he bestows predictions upon them both far and near.

Those who do not observe skillfully do not believe that the mind possesses all the marks; rather, one should follow those who observe according to reality and believe that the mind possesses all the marks.

This is the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). Regarding such "nature" (*prakṛti*), nature refers to that which is internal; it generally possesses three meanings. First, it is called "nature" in the sense of being unchanging;

the *Avyākṛta-sūtra* (Wuxing jing) speaks of "immovable nature," wherein nature has the meaning of being unchanging. Furthermore, "nature" is named as "nature-portion" (*prakṛti-bhāga*), in the sense of a category or class.

The divisions are distinct; each cannot be altered. Furthermore, nature (*xing*) is the true nature (*shixing*). True nature is precisely the principle-nature (*lixing*). Being the ultimate reality, it is beyond reproach;
it is merely another name for Buddha-nature (*foxing*). The immovable nature supports emptiness (*kong*); the seed-nature (*zhongxing*) supports the provisional (*jia*);

the true nature supports the Middle Way (*zhong*). Now, it is clarified that the internal nature cannot be altered, just as the fire-nature within bamboo, though invisible, cannot be said not to exist.
There is none. Just as the fire-drill burns all dry grass, the mind is likewise: though it possesses the nature of all five aggregates and is invisible, one cannot say it does not exist;
when observed with the eye of wisdom, it is seen to possess all natures.

Regarding "such substance" (*tattva*): it is called "substance" because it is the basis for arising. These aggregates (*skandha*) of the ten dharma-realms all take matter and mind as their substantial essence.

Regarding "such power" (*bala*): it refers to the capacity for functional efficacy. It is like a king or a strongman who is capable of wearing thousands or tens of thousands [of armor]; it is so called because of illness.
There is none. When an illness has been cured, it becomes functional; the mind is also like this. It possesses all powers, yet because of the illness of the afflictions (*kleśa*), it cannot move.
If one contemplates it as it truly is, one sees that it is endowed with all powers.
Thus, that which acts is established as "action. Apart from the mind, there is nothing further that acts;
therefore, one knows that the mind possesses all action.
Regarding such causes: that which draws forth a fruit serves as the cause and is also termed "karma. The karma of the ten dharma realms arises from the mind;
as long as there is a mind, all karmas are fully present. Therefore, it is called "such a cause."
Regarding "condition" (*pratyaya*) in this context: it means the basis of conditioning. All factors that assist karma possess the sense of being conditions.
Ignorance, craving, and so forth, which are able to moisten karma, take the mind as their condition.
Regarding such results: they are obtained as results. The causal habituation continues from the preceding moment, while the resultant habituation is obtained in the subsequent moment;
therefore, it is called "such a result."

Regarding "retribution" (*vipāka*): to recompense a cause is called retribution. The causal habituation and the resultant habituation are both collectively termed "cause," as they draw forth the retribution of future lives;
this retribution is what compensates for the cause.
Regarding the statement that "the beginning and the end are ultimately equal": the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are the beginning and the retribution (*vipāka*) is the end.

Both the beginning and the end arise from conditions; because they arise from conditions, they are empty. Since both the beginning and the end are empty, this constitutes equality in terms of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Furthermore, characteristics are merely words, and retribution is also merely words;
both are provisionally established. This constitutes equality in terms of conventional designation (*prajñapti*). Moreover, the beginning and the end mutually represent one another.

The banner: one examines the initial signs to know the subsequent retribution; observing the subsequent retribution, one knows the original signs. It is like seeing charity and knowing wealth, or seeing wealth and knowing charity; the initial and subsequent signs exist together.
This is an equality discussed from the perspective of conventional designation (*prajñapti*). Furthermore, regarding signs and signlessness: it is signless yet characterized by signs.
Neither having marks nor being markless; retribution and non-retribution; non-retribution yet retribution;
neither retribution nor non-retribution—each and every one enters the limit of reality (*tathatā*). This is the equality discussed herein.

Regarding the second type of interpretation: the ten factors are grouped into four categories. The three miserable realms take suffering as their characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), the fixed accumulation of evil as their nature (*svabhāva*), the crushing of form and mind as their essence (*tattva*), the ascent of blades and entry into cauldrons as their power (*bala*), and the arousal of the ten unwholesome actions as their activity (*kriyā*).
With tainted unwholesome karma as the cause, craving, grasping, and so forth as the conditions, the fruit of unwholesome habituation as the result, and the three evil destinies as the retribution—
the ignorance that pervades both the beginning and the end constitutes the equality [of these factors].

The three wholesome manifest actions have joy as their characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). The collection of meditative wholesomeness is their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Their essence (*tattva*) consists of the emergence of the body and mind. Pleasant sensation (*sukha-vedanā*) is their power (*bala*).
The undertaking of the five precepts and ten wholesome paths is their activity (*kriyā*). Wholesome karma is their cause (*hetu*). Wholesome craving and grasping are their conditions (*pratyaya*).

The fruit of wholesome cultivation is their result (*phala*). Rebirth among humans and devas is their retribution (*vipāka*). They should be understood according to conventional designations (*prajñapti*). Their equality (*samatā*) consists in the presence of these characteristics from beginning to end.

In the case of the Two Vehicles (the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas), they take *nirvāṇa* as their characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), liberation as their nature (*svabhāva*), the five factors as their substance (*tattva*), non-bondage as their power (*bala*),

the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) as their activity (*kriyā*), untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) as their cause (*hetu*), the practice of cultivation (*bhāvanā*) as their condition (*pratyaya*), and the four fruits as their result (*phala*).
Since these do not arise again within the field of subsequent existence, they are said to be without retribution (*avipāka*), and so forth.

Regarding the Bodhisattva as a category of Buddha: the conditioning cause (*pratyaya-hetu*) is its characteristic; the understanding cause (*pariniṣpatti-hetu*) is its nature; the direct cause (*samyak-hetu*) is its essence; the four great vows are its power;
the six perfections and myriad practices are its function; the adornment of wisdom is its cause; the adornment of merit is its condition;
the three types of enlightenment (*trividha-bodhi*) are its fruit; and Great Nirvana is its retribution, and so forth.

The world of sentient beings is a mere provisional designation; it has no substantial essence and is a conceptual construction, established as a conventional fiction by gathering together real dharmas.

That is to say: the sentient beings of the evil realms are ultimately equal in their characteristics, nature, substance, and form, and so forth. The sentient beings of the good realms are ultimately equal in their characteristics, nature, substance, and power.
The untainted sentient beings are ultimately equal in their characteristics, nature, substance, and power. This applies equally to Bodhisattvas and the Buddha-dharmas.
The realms (*dhātu*), characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), nature (*svabhāva*), power (*bala*), and ultimate essence (*niṣṭhā*) are all to be understood by analogy with this.
The world of lands (*kṣetra-loka*) also possesses ten kinds of dharmas, namely:

the characteristics, nature, power, and so forth of evil lands, as well as those of virtuous lands, untainted lands (*anāsrava-kṣetra*), and the lands of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, including their characteristics, nature, power, and so forth.
Now, a single mind possesses the ten dharma-realms; each individual dharma-realm, in turn, possesses the ten dharma-realms, making one hundred dharma-realms.
Each realm possesses thirty kinds of worlds, so that one hundred dharma-realms possess three thousand kinds of worlds.

These three thousand worlds exist within a single thought-moment (*citta-kṣaṇa*). If there were no mind, they would simply not exist; yet, with even a minute flicker of mind, the three thousand are immediately present. Furthermore, it is not said that they are identical to the one [mind].
The mind comes first; all phenomena follow. Nor can it be said that all phenomena come first and the single mind follows.

For example, when an object undergoes the eight phases of change: if the object were prior to the phases, the object would not be subject to change; if the phases were prior to the object, the phases themselves would not be subject to change.
It is neither possible for the former nor for the latter. Rather, one speaks of the phases changing with respect to the object, and one speaks of the object with respect to the changing phases.
The mind now is also like this. If all phenomena arise from a single mind, this would be vertical (longitudinal).
If the mind simultaneously contains all phenomena, this would be horizontal (transverse). Verticality is untenable; horizontality is also untenable.
It is simply that the mind is all phenomena, and all phenomena are the mind; therefore, it is neither vertical nor horizontal, neither one nor different. Profound.

It is wondrous, profound, and absolute; it is not that which is known by consciousness, nor is it that which can be expressed by words. This is why it is called the "inconceivable realm" (acintya-viṣaya);
the meaning lies herein.
It is like the wish-fulfilling jewel (cintāmaṇi), a supreme treasure of the heavens, which, though as small as a mustard seed, possesses great power to provide the five pure and subtle desires.
The seven treasures and *linglang* jewels do not come from within nor enter from without; they are not premeditated in their sequence, nor are they selected for quantity;
they are not fashioned as coarse or exquisite, yet they fall in profuse abundance according to one’s needs, neither increasing nor exhausting.

Since even these material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) can manifest in such a way, how much more so the spirit and mind, which are numinous and wondrous—how could they not possess all dharmas? Furthermore, when the three poisons delude the mind, [the first...]
When the mind of mindfulness arises, there still remain the eighty-eight afflictions (*anuśaya*)—both sharp and dull—along with the eighty-four thousand afflictions.
If one says they existed beforehand, why do they wait for conditions? If one says they were originally non-existent, how can they manifest when confronted by conditions?

They are neither existent nor non-existent; to hold them as definitely existent is heterodox, and to hold them as definitely non-existent is delusive. One should know that they exist while not existing, and do not exist while existing; this is what is meant by "delusion" (*moha*).

If even the ordinary mind is thus, how much more so the inconceivable single mind? Furthermore, it is like a dream: one may see hundreds of thousands of things, yet upon waking, not a single one remains.
How much less could there be hundreds of thousands? When not asleep, not dreaming, and not awakened, there is neither multiplicity nor unity.

It is by the power of sleep that one speaks of "many," and by the power of awakening that one speaks of "few. Zhuang Zhou dreamed he was a butterfly, fluttering for a hundred years; upon waking, he knew it was not so.
A butterfly does not exist through the accumulation of years; the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) within the dharma of ignorance is the one mind within all minds.
Just as in a state of deep sleep, one realizes that ignorance is itself the nature of phenomena; all minds are the one mind. This is like awakening from sleep, and so forth.

Furthermore, for a practitioner who practices with ease, a single dream during sleep encompasses everything from the initial aspiration for enlightenment (prathamacittotpāda) up to sitting at the site of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa), turning the wheel of Dharma, and delivering sentient beings.
One enters nirvana while still alive; one suddenly awakens to realize that it was but a single dream-event. If one believes these three parables, then one believes in the One Mind.
It cannot be proclaimed by words nor fathomed by the intellect. Within this inconceivable realm, what dharma is not subsumed? This realm gives rise to wisdom.
What wisdom would not arise? Relying on this object, one makes a vow; even until there is no longer craving for dharmas (*dharmatṛṣṇā*).

What vow would not be complete? What practice would not be fulfilled? When explained, it follows the sequence mentioned above; when practiced, all minds are contained within a single mind (and so forth).
Regarding the arousal of the bodhicitta:
one who arouses the true and correct bodhicitta has already deeply realized the inconceivable realm and understands that one suffering is all sufferings.

They feel personal sorrow for their past sufferings—how they were deluded and immersed in coarse and base forms and sounds, and how they abandoned restraint over body, speech, and mind to commit unwholesome karmas.
The wheel revolves through the evil realms, entangling one in various burning afflictions; with physical and mental suffering, one brings about self-destruction.
Now, once again, one is bound by the cocoon of craving and harmed by the lamp of ignorance. For hundreds of thousands of myriads of kalpas—how painful this is!

Even if one wishes to abandon the three miserable paths and delights in the five precepts and ten wholesome actions, cultivating merit with a calculating mind is like bartering at a marketplace; it only serves to increase one’s transgressions all the more.
Like a fish entering the mouth of a basket, or a moth rushing into a lamp; their frantic schemes and perverse cleverness lead them ever more lost and ever further astray.
Thirsting, they drink salt water; dragon-whiskers entwine their bodies; entering the water only increases their agony. Ox-hide binds their limbs; facing the sun, it becomes even more rigid.

Like a blind man entering a thicket of thorns, or drowning in a swirling eddy; embracing blades and grasping torches—their pain is beyond description. With tiger tails and serpent heads, they tremble in terror and lamentation.
I am struck with awe. I grieve for myself in this way; I grieve for others in the same manner.

Suppose one were to flee from a hostile country through narrow paths, enduring every hardship, fainting and then reviving again, until finally reaching a poor village where one works for hire for a single day and stays overnight in a thatched hut—refusing to advance further, delighting instead in such base affairs, lacking faith and understanding, which is both pitiable and strange. Contemplating them and myself, my heart is choked with pain.
He immediately gave rise to great compassion and made two vows: "I vow to deliver infinite sentient beings; I vow to sever innumerable afflictions.
Although sentient beings are like empty space, he vows to deliver those sentient beings who are like empty space;
although he knows that afflictions are non-existent, he vows to sever those non-existent afflictions; and although he knows the number of sentient beings is exceedingly vast, he delivers them.
There are exceedingly many sentient beings who, although they know that afflictions are bottomless, sever those bottomless afflictions;

who, although they know that the suchness of sentient beings is identical to the suchness of the Buddha, deliver those sentient beings whose suchness is identical to the Buddha’s suchness; and who, although they know that afflictions are the true mark of reality (*tathatā-lakṣaṇa*), sever those afflictions that are the true mark of reality.
Why is this? Because if one were merely to uproot the cause of suffering without uprooting [the underlying nature], [it would not be liberation].

[The text continues: "The fruit [of this vow] is mixed with poison; therefore, one must contemplate emptiness (*śūnyatā*). If one contemplates emptiness exclusively, one will not see sentient beings who can be saved;

such a person is called 'one who clings to emptiness' and cannot be transformed by the Buddhas. If one sees only that there are sentient beings to be saved, one falls into 'great compassion based on attachment and views' (*sneha-dṛṣṭi-mahākaruṇā*), which is not the path of liberation, and so forth. Now, because it is neither poisonous nor false, it is called 'true. It is not..."

The limit of emptiness is not a finite limit; therefore, it is called "correct. It is like a bird flying through the sky: it ultimately does not abide in the sky. Although it does not abide in the sky, its tracks cannot be sought.
Though it traverses the sky, it does so within emptiness; though it traverses, it remains empty. For this reason, it is said that one "vows to contend with empty space.
This is precisely what is meant by the true and correct arousal of the bodhicitta. This is the intended meaning.

Furthermore, one contemplates the inconceivable mind of consciousness: the single mind of bliss and the all-pervading mind of bliss. Although I and all sentient beings have sought happiness in the past, we did not know the cause of happiness;
it was like grasping at pebbles and rubble while calling them wish-fulfilling jewels, or mistakenly pointing to the glow of fireflies and shouting that they were the sun and moon.
Only now do I finally understand this, and thus I give rise to great compassion and establish two vows, namely: "The infinite vows regarding the Dharma-gates."
Know this: I vow to attain the unsurpassed path of the Buddha. Although I know that the Dharma-gates are eternally quiescent like space, I vow to practice that eternal quiescence.
Although I know that Bodhi is non-existent, yet within this non-existence, I nevertheless seek it.
Although I know that the Dharma-gates are like space and non-existent, I vow to paint, embroider, and adorn empty space. Although I know that the Buddha-way is not...
The accomplished and that which is to be accomplished are like planting a tree in empty space, causing it to flower and bear fruit.

Although one knows the Dharma-gates and the fruit of Buddhahood, one cultivates them through neither cultivation nor non-cultivation; one realizes and attains them through neither realization nor attainment, because there is nothing to be realized or attained.
This is called "true" because it is neither false nor poisonous; it is called "correct" because it is neither emptiness nor the craving of views. Thus it is.
Compassionate vows and inconceivable realm-and-wisdom arise simultaneously, neither before nor after;
compassion is itself wisdom, and wisdom is itself compassion. Without conditions and without thought, it universally covers all, spontaneously uprooting suffering and naturally bestowing bliss.
It is not like poison or harm, not merely empty, and not like attachment or views. This is called the True.
The meaning of Bodhi as the initial arousal of the right resolve has already been explained through compassion for oneself. The meaning of compassion for sentient beings is all as stated above.
Regarding "skillful settling of the mind":
skillful settling of the mind means skillfully establishing [the mind] within the *dharmatā* by means of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. This refers to the profound realization of the inconceivable.

The realm is profound, abstruse, subtle, and secret. Its vast exercise of compassion extends like a canopy such as this; one must practice to fulfill its vow. Practice is precisely *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
Ignorance and delusive confusion are, in their essence, *dharmatā*; because of delusion and bewilderment, *dharmatā* transforms into ignorance.
Various inversions arise—such as the wholesome and the unwholesome—just as cold causes water to congeal and transform into solid ice, or as sleep causes the mind to transform into various dreams.
Now one should realize that these inversions are themselves the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena), neither identical nor different [from it].
Although inversions arise and cease like a whirling firebrand, do not believe in the arising and ceasing of inversions; believe only in this mind.

However, this is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). Arising is the arising of the nature of phenomena; ceasing is the ceasing of the nature of phenomena. In reality, there is neither arising nor ceasing;

what is falsely called arising and ceasing is merely the pointing out of deluded thoughts, all of which are entirely the nature of phenomena. Binding the nature of phenomena with the nature of phenomena, and contemplating the nature of phenomena with the nature of phenomena, it is always the nature of phenomena.
When one realizes that there is never a time when it is not the nature of phenomena, and this realization of its essence is established, one must not fall into delusion.

One contemplates and likewise does not apprehend the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). Returning to the source and reverting to the root, the entire dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is simultaneously stilled; this is called *śamatha*.
When one abides in such *śamatha*, all the aforementioned processes of transmigration are brought to rest.
As for "contemplation": it is the observation that the mind of ignorance, when viewed from above, is equal to the *dharmatā*—primordially empty;

Regarding the "Great Exposition of the Dharma-numbers of the Four *Siddhāntas*": *siddha* means "universal" (*sarva*). *Siddhānta* is a Sanskrit term; in its full form it is *dāna*, which in this context means "giving" (*śī*). This is a combination of Chinese and Sanskrit.
Because it encompasses these [meanings], it is called *siddhānta*. The Buddha preaches the Dharma by means of these four, bestowing them universally upon all sentient beings;
therefore, they are named the Four *Siddhāntas*. First is the *loka-siddhānta*. "World" (*loka*) signifies the sense of separation and distinction; "realm" (*siddhānta*) signifies a delimited sphere.

This is because the faculties and capacities (*indriya-bhājana*) of sentient beings are shallow; therefore, the Buddha, in accordance with what they desire and delight in hearing, explains it by means of sequential distinctions to inspire joy in them.

This is called the *loka-prasiddha-siddhānta* (the universal standpoint). Second is the *pudgala-prasiddha-siddhānta* (the individual standpoint), which means that when the Buddha wishes to preach the Dharma, he must first observe the magnitude of the sentient beings' faculties and the depth of their past seeds, and only then [proceed].

He teaches according to their individual capacities, causing them to give rise to right faith and increase their roots of goodness; therefore, this is called the *puruṣa-siddhānta* (the doctrine for individuals).
Third is the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (the therapeutic doctrine), which means: knowing that a sentient being has much desire, he instructs them to contemplate impurity;

knowing they have much hatred, he instructs them to contemplate loving-kindness; and knowing they have much delusion, he instructs them to contemplate dependent origination. For these various [cases of] imbalance...
Regarding illness, he expounds this medicinal Dharma and bestows it universally upon all sentient beings; therefore, it is called the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (the standpoint of therapeutic remedy).

Fourth is the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (the standpoint of ultimate truth). "Ultimate truth" refers to the principle (*tattva*). This means that when the Tathāgata perceives that the roots of goodness in sentient beings have matured, he immediately expounds the Dharma for them, enabling them to realize the Noble Path; this is called the *paramārtha-siddhānta*.

The *Miaozongchao* states: "Because the capacities [of sentient beings] vary in being raw or mature, they are reached by the four *siddhāntas*. For those who have not yet planted [the seeds], a worldly teaching (*loka-siddhānta*) is provided to cause them to desire [the Dharma];
